en: The two middle sūtras state:
"A Bodhisattva who practices the ten wholesome actions and generates the Great Mind forever departs from the ocean of the suffering wheel of the triple world;

those with middling or lower grades of the ten wholesome actions become minor regional kings (*kṣullakarāja*), while those with the superior grade become Iron-Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*). The commentary explains: "The ten wholesome [actions]..."
As follows:
In these stages of the ten wholesome paths, one enters the stage of "subdued patience" (*kṣānti*) only after ten thousand kalpas, because this is the skillful means of patience.

That which is called "arousing the great mind" (*mahācittotpāda*) is so named because that which is to be saved, that which is to be severed, that which is to be cultivated, and that which is to be attained are all vast.
Regarding "permanently departing from the three realms": those who previously generated the Great Resolve are generally of two types:
first, those who proceed directly; second, those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
If one has previously generated the resolve suddenly and abruptly, the mind will necessarily be firm and fierce; for although afflictions have not yet been severed, one is certain to transcend them.

If one subsequently attains gradual awakening, the fruits of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles—both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—involve the severance of obstacles through the Noble Path; this is because they are said to be permanently separated [from saṃsāra].

As for the "ocean of the wheel of suffering," suffering pervades the three realms, namely the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*); it is established as suffering based on the feelings of pain, pleasure, and equanimity.
They come and go without ceasing, revolving like a wheel; they rise and sink, emerging and submerging with a depth and vastness like the ocean.

As for those of middling and lower grades of goodness, because the duration of their cultivation of the ten wholesome paths is long, these constitute the lower, middle, and upper stages according to their initial, intermediate, and final phases.
Those of the middle and lower grades become *kṣullaka-rāja* (scattered-rice kings); because their numerous minor kings are like scattered grains of rice, they are so named after this metaphor.
Furthermore, as for those who divided the fragrant rice at the beginning of the kalpa, they were called *kṣullaka-rāja* because they distributed the rice like scattered grains.
If it is of the highest grade, one is an Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).
From this point, the third section clarifies the stages of the three types of noble persons (*śaikṣa*).
The Sūtra says:

"Those of the lineage of practice possess the copper wheel over two worlds; those of the lineage of nature possess the silver wheel over three worlds; and the wheel-turning kings of the firm virtues of the factors of enlightenment possess the golden wheel over four worlds with its seven treasures."
The commentary states:

Bodhisattvas in the ten stages (bhūmi) become copper-wheel kings; those in the ten practices (caryā) become silver-wheel kings; and those in the stage of the ten dedications (pariṇāmanā) become gold-wheel kings.

Regarding the distinctions in the sovereign transformation of these four types of wheel-turning kings, they differ according to whether their realm of influence consists of one, two, three, or four continents.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "From the time when the lifespan of the people of this continent is immeasurable down to eighty thousand years, there arise Wheel-turning Kings (*cakravartin*).

When [the lifespan] decreases from eighty thousand years, sentient beings suffer a decline in wealth, happiness, and longevity; as various evils gradually increase, they are no longer vessels for great men, and thus there are no Wheel-turning Kings."

This king, who leads and guides by means of the revolving wheel and subdues all through his majesty, is called a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), distinguished by the specific wheels of gold, silver, copper, or iron.

If a king is born of the Kṣatriya caste, having succeeded to the consecrated position, on the fifteenth day when he observes the fast, having bathed his head and body and undertaken the supreme fast, he ascends a high palace terrace attended by his ministers; then, suddenly from the east, the precious wheel-treasure appears.
It should be understood that the same applies to all other wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*).
As with the Buddha, no two wheel-turning kings appear simultaneously.

All wheel-turning kings are free from violence; having subdued their opponents and brought them to victory, they establish each in their own dwelling and exhort them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).

As for what are called the seven treasures, they are the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander treasure.
The five treasures, such as the horse and so forth, are comprised of sentient beings, whereas the two treasures—the jewel and the wheel—are insentient.

Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* mentions seven treasures, namely: the sword treasure, the skin treasure, the bed treasure, the grove treasure, the palace treasure, the garment treasure, and the footwear treasure. All of these various treasures are summoned through the cultivation of the wholesome root of non-aversion.
All matters concerning majesty and virtue, as well as the royal governance and social transformation, are explained in detail in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* and the *Lokotpatti-sūtra*.
From this point, the second section provides a general explanation of the "Patience of Submission" (*kṣānti*).
Within this, there are now three sections;
first, the initial section provides a general explanation of the "sacred embryo" (āryagarbha).
The Sūtra states:

“The thirty stages of the noble embryo of the patience of submissiveness—namely, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten transferences—are those in which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have trained; there are none who do not arise from this patience of submissiveness.”
The commentary states:
Abiding in the patience of acquiescence (*kṣānti*) is precisely what is called the "sacred embryo" (*āryagarbha*), for all Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from it.
This second section clarifies the difficulty of entering [this state].
Sūtra:

“The root of all bodhisattva practices is therefore the generation of the mind and the attainment of faith; if one attains this faith, one will certainly not regress and will enter the first stage of the path of non-arising.”
The commentary states:
Regarding "the root of all bodhisattva practices," this clarifies the fundamental basis for the bodhisattva practice of entering the kalpas, which is the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).

This mind is difficult to arouse; as the preceding sutra says, "Though there be those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who see the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, those who succeed in entering faith are exceedingly few."

If one attains the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and does not regress from the sixth mind onward, this is called "non-retrogression through faith" (*śraddhā-avaivartika*), because one will certainly realize non-arising (*anutpāda*) and reach the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Although there is the possibility of turning toward the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) prior to the seventh dwelling (*saptamī vihāra*), even if that occurs, it will not last long, for one will certainly attain [the higher stages] before long.
Another interpretation is as follows:

If one attains the mind of faith, one will certainly not regress from the ten stages of faith; however, while the seventh stage of the ten abidings constitutes non-regression, there remains the possibility of regression prior to that point.

As the *Sutra of the Necklaces* states: "The Devaputra Viśuddhanetra, the Prince Dharmamati, Śāriputra, and others wished to enter the seventh stage, but they retreated due to encountering adverse conditions."
From this third point, the definition of the characteristics is established.
The Sūtra states:
"To bring about the transformation and benefit of both self and others with complete equality—this is called the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind."
The commentary states:
"Transforming and benefiting oneself and others" explains the characteristics of the arousal of the bodhicitta.

When a bodhisattva regards others as themselves and, having attained a mind of equality, cultivates the two benefits, this is precisely what is called the characteristic of the bodhisattva’s initial arousal of the mind entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The explanation of the Patience of Submission (*kṣānti*) is concluded.
From here follows the second section, consisting of five lines and a half, which extensively explains the Patience of Clarity (*viśuddha-kṣānti*).
This is divided into two parts:
First, the three stages are explained individually; second, the elimination of obstacles is summarized.
Regarding the initial explanation of the three stages, the text is divided into three parts.
First, the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) is explained, which is further divided into three sections:
Furthermore, first, the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), is elucidated in the Sūtra:

"The Bodhisattva King of the Wheel-Turning Joyfully illuminates for the first time the principle of the equality of the two truths; through skillful transformation, he travels among a hundred kingdoms, and with pure generosity, he benefits all sentient beings."
The commentary states:
"Joyful" and so forth indicates the name of the stage of dwelling (*vihāra*) and clarifies its royal status.
"First illuminating the principle of the equality of the two truths" means that this [stage] first realizes the equality of *tathatā* (suchness), thereby severing conceptual discrimination.
"Temporarily transforming sentient beings" means that he may manifest as a king or a Buddha through the power of expedient transformation.
"Wandering through a hundred kingdoms" clarifies the scope of his transformative influence.
"The purity of the perfection of giving" refers to his superior practice of benefiting living beings.
From this, the second [stage] is explained as being named "The Ground of Illumination" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
The Sūtra states:
"Wisdom that enters into principle is called 'abiding' (*vihāra*); the arising of virtuous qualities from that abiding is called a 'ground' (*bhūmi*)."
The commentary states:
"Entering" means realization.
Regarding the term *prajñā*, both the non-conceptual wisdom that realizes the principle of true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) and [the wisdom associated with it] are called *prajñā*.
"Abiding" (sthiti) means being unmoving; it carries the sense of a support or foundation.

Regarding "abiding gives rise to virtuous qualities and is thus called a 'ground'": when wisdom merges with ultimate truth, it is able to give rise to and manifest unconditioned virtues; conditioned merits arise because of this, and unconditioned merits are manifested because of this.
Because it manifests the two meanings of abiding and arising through the five characteristics, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*); these are the ten grounds of the path.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, chapter nine, states: "Thus, these ten grounds collectively subsume all conditioned and unconditioned merits as their intrinsic nature."
Because it serves as the superior support for the practices one cultivates, enabling them to grow and flourish, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).
From this point, the third stage, the Initial Mind endowed with virtues, is described in the Sūtra:
"The first dwelling possesses all virtues within a single mind, remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth.
The commentary states:
Regarding the "first dwelling," the realization of suchness upon the path of seeing is designated as the first dwelling.
"Single-mindedness" refers to the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the one mind.
"Possessing all virtues" is as stated in the aforementioned sutra: "fully endowed with eighty-four thousand virtues."
Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the locative case ending (the seventh sound) indicates that wisdom realizes true tranquility without wavering.
This refers to the initial entry into the [first] stage (*bhūmi*); subsequent cases should be understood by analogy.
Following this, the second section clarifies medium-level patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*).
This section is divided into two parts;
first, the explanation of the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
The Sūtra states:

The Bodhisattva Vigatamala, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, manifests his form throughout the six realms and a thousand lands; having fully perfected the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline, he is forever free from the faults of transgressions and errors.
The commentary states:
By designating the name of the land, it clarifies the dwelling place of the King, clarifies the realm of those to be transformed, and clarifies the cultivation of supreme practices.
Through the perfection of the *pāramitā* of ethical discipline (*śīla*), it clarifies his freedom from transgressions, such that he does not violate even the most subtle precepts.
From this point, the second section clarifies the cultivation of the object and wisdom.
The Sūtra states:
"The true nature is signless and objectless; it is without substance, without arising, and is illuminated as non-dual."
The commentary states:

The first phrase clarifies the object (*viṣaya*), because one falsely clings to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as being distinct from the dependently originated perfected nature (*paratantra-pariniṣpanna*).

The second phrase clarifies wisdom (*jñāna*): it is because one realizes the absence of intrinsic essence, understands non-arising, and realizes non-duality; thus, the illumination of wisdom brings about liberation through the absence of conceptual differentiation.
Although there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority among the five patiences (*kṣānti*), one should understand that their objects and wisdoms correspond accordingly.
Third, this explains the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*).
The Sūtra says:

The Bodhisattva Radiant Light, King of the Yāma Heaven, manifests his form to travel to ten thousand Buddha-fields; he is skillfully able to penetrate samādhi, appearing and disappearing with mastery, and possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge.
The commentary states:

By designating the name of the land, it clarifies the dwelling place of the King, clarifies the realm of those to be transformed, clarifies his attainment of meditative concentration, and clarifies the virtues he possesses.

Regarding the "hidden and manifest," this refers to his mastery of the five supernormal powers and his possession of the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), as described in the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).
From this, the second summary of the severance of hindrances follows.
The Sūtra states:

"The Joyful, the Stainless, and the Radiant [stages] can extinguish the afflictions that bind one to form; they fully observe all bodily and vocal actions, and the purity of the dharma-nature shines forth in perfect fullness."
The commentary states:

This explains that the three stages mentioned above are able to sever the fetters of form (*rūpa-bandhana*), namely the three [afflictions] such as craving (*rāga*) and so forth, as explained previously.
"Fully observing all actions of body and speech" manifests the departure from the fetters of form and the mastery over formative actions (*rūpa-karman*).
Regarding the term "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*): the true nature of form and mind is precisely *tathatā* (suchness), which is the perfection of the illumination of wisdom.
Following this, there are four verses in the third section that extensively clarify compliant patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
This section is divided into two parts:
first, a detailed explanation of the three stages; second, a summary of the abandonment of hindrances.
The initial explanation of the three stages is further divided into three sections:
Furthermore, first is the elucidation of the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The Sūtra states:

"The Bodhisattva Arciṣmatī, of great diligence, as a King of Tuṣita Heaven, travels through billions of lands; with the wisdom of ultimate reality (*bhūtajñāna*) and the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*), he realizes the principle of non-arising and illuminates both emptiness and existence."
The commentary states:
This indicates the name of the land, clarifying that it is where supreme practices are cultivated and where the Vidyārāja dwells.
"Ultimate wisdom and quiescence" refers to the realization of the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*).
The wisdom of skillful means is the wisdom that takes phenomena as its object.
That which penetrates the principle of non-arising is the realm of true suchness and correct wisdom.
That which illuminates both emptiness and existence is the realm of the skillful means of principle and phenomena.
From here, the second stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjaya), is elucidated.
The Sūtra states:

“The Bodhisattva of the Difficult to Conquer attains equanimity; as the king of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, he oversees ten billion realms. Through the profound contemplation of emptiness within emptiness, he perceives no dualistic characteristics; manifesting his form throughout the six destinies, there is nowhere he does not pervade.”
The commentary states:

This indicates the name of the land and clarifies the cultivation of the correct contemplation. Because the activities of the two wisdoms—the ultimate and the conventional—are mutually opposed, they are brought into union and made to correspond; hence it is called "Equilibrium.
This clarifies the dwelling place of the King.

Regarding "thoroughly contemplating emptiness within emptiness": the initial emptiness reveals suchness (*tathatā*), while the subsequent emptiness dispels characteristics—whether these be referred to as form and mind, or self and phenomena.
It is said that within this stage, principle and phenomena are in harmonious correspondence; hence, it is called "thorough contemplation."
Regarding "the mark of non-duality": it is able to harmonize that which is difficult to harmonize and bring them into correspondence, because it possesses the mark of non-duality.
"Descending in form" below clarifies the realm of those to be transformed.
"Mi" means "none."
From here, the third stage, the Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī*), is explained.
The Sūtra says:

"The Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Presence perceives that the characteristics of dependent origination are non-dual; the light of ultimate wisdom is able to pervade everywhere, proceeding to a thousand billion lands to transform sentient beings."
The commentary states:
"Marking the name of the land clarifies the dwelling place of the King.
'Illuminatively seeing dependent origination' means that wisdom constantly illuminates and understands the non-duality of the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination."
Regarding "the light of ultimate wisdom": wisdom that takes the ultimate truth as its object is called "ultimate wisdom.
Because this wisdom can illuminate the principle, it is termed "light-power.
Because its illumination and understanding are perfect in essence, it is said to be "pervasive and all-encompassing."
Because he travels to billions of lands to manifest his transformative power.
This is the second summary, concluding the section on severing hindrances.
The Sūtra says:

The stages of Arciṣmatī, Sudurjayā, and Abhimukhī can sever the delusions of the mind that obscure the three obstacles; through the tranquil wisdom of emptiness and objectless contemplation, they reflect back upon the infinite realm of the mind's own emptiness.
The commentary states:

"To 'summarize the three higher stages' means that those capable of severing the delusions of the mind regarding the three obstacles are, as mentioned above, the three types of obstacles such as the obstacle of views."
"Speaking of the wisdom of emptiness" refers to the realization of the fruit of knowledge.
"Speaking of tranquility" refers to the realization of equality.
"Non-conditioned contemplation" refers to the realization that the characteristics of dependent origination are non-dual.
Regarding "returning to illuminate the emptiness of the mind": since one's own obscurations have been severed, one illuminates the suchness (*tathatā*) of one’s own stage.
Because the merit of this wisdom of suchness is vast, it is called "immeasurable.
From here, the fourth [stage] has two and a half lines that clarify the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*).
This section is divided into three parts;
first, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (The Far-Reaching Ground) is explained.
Sūtra:

The Bodhisattva Dūraga, King of the First Dhyāna, abides in the patience of signlessness and non-arising; through skillful means that are entirely impartial, he constantly transforms sentient beings across ten billion lands.
The commentary states:
By designating the name of the land, the dwelling place of the King is clarified.

Regarding "the patience of signlessness and non-arising," because the Bodhisattvas of this stage consist solely of signless contemplation, it is said that they realize the patience of non-arising through signless wisdom.
"Skillful means" refers to clearly practicing superior conduct in order to benefit and deliver sentient beings with complete impartiality.
From "constantly [acting] for the myriad [beings]" onwards, it clarifies the objects of conversion.
From this point, one transcends the second type of birth, that of segmented existence.
As the Sūtra says:
"Having entered the stage of the flow of the immovable dharma, one is forever free from segmented existence and transcends all realms of being."
The commentary states:
A Bodhisattva on this stage will certainly be able to enter the subsequent Immovable Stage (*aniñjyā bhūmi*), which is like a swift current.
Regarding "not yet being free from the segmented [existence]": prior to this stage, there may still be segmented existence, whereby one undergoes birth within the three realms.
Now, because this stage within the realm of effort (*prayoga*) marks the very end of the divisions,

those who transcend all states of existence (*bhava*) do so by means of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and vows (*praṇidhāna*) which support that superior body, causing the retributive result it receives to gradually increase in excellence until, at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*sambodhi*), one undergoes the birth of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*) and thus transcends the three realms of existence.
From this, the third section clarifies the obstacles to be abandoned.
The Sūtra states:

"Constantly contemplating the ultimate truth, illuminating non-duality, and practicing the twenty-one modes of emptiness and quiescence, the Bodhisattva on the stage of Far-Going alone is able to sever the habitual tendencies of ignorance regarding the craving for dharmas that accord with the Path."
The commentary states:
"Constantly observing" indicates that there is no interruption.
"Ultimate truth" clarifies that which is realized.
"Shining upon the non-dual" means that the ultimate and conventional truths are illuminated simultaneously, such that there is no duality between them.
"Twenty-one births" clarifies the births within the sūtra.
There are three [types of] births for each stage (*bhūmi*); now, in the seventh stage, one undergoes twenty-one births as described in the sūtra.
Wisdom illuminates all as suchness; this is called the practice of emptiness and quiescence.
In reality, there are twenty births within the stages of abiding; because one will certainly attain [the goal] upon the final birth.
"Affection for the dharmas that accord with the Path" refers to affection for wholesome dharmas.
In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is called "desire for wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "At the stage of the 'Summits' (*mūrdhan*), one has not yet subdued the attachment to dharmas that accord with the Path; it does not say [this attachment] is severed at the stage of 'Patience' (*kṣānti*)."
Regarding this statement on "severance": it means that prior to the sixth stage, there is both concentration and distraction, and craving arises during states of distraction.

Now, although one applies effort upon entering this stage, because the continuity of the signless (*animitta*) manifests before them, there is no distracted longing; since craving is forever absent, [craving] is severed.
Regarding the "habitual tendency of ignorance," as the sutra below states: "severing the subtle manifestations of all karmic fruits.
These "karmic fruits" refer precisely to birth within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti*).
The subtle manifestation of activity is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Clinging to the manifestation of subtle marks of arising and ceasing can obstruct the wondrous path of signlessness (*animitta*) of this stage.
The essence of the cognitive obscuration is ignorance (*avidyā*); it coexists with the aforementioned craving and is abandoned upon entering this stage.
Therefore, the verse says: "Only the Great Being who has traveled far can sever [them].

In the preceding prose section, the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages are all treated as a single passage concerning the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of both form and mind.

Regarding this separate conclusion (*pṛthag-nigamana*): it is because one has forever transcended craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) and the arising of the limited分段生 (*paricchinna-janman*), reaching the final limit of effort (*prayoga-paryanta*).
Since it possesses these three meanings, it is concluded separately.
Furthermore, if the great eons (*mahākalpa*) are counted as three incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), now the second of these incalculable aeons is completed at the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the latter two [stages] are identical to the third stage in that they are all characterized by effortlessness; therefore, they are grouped together.
From this point, the fifth section contains five verses clarifying the three subsequent stages.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the specific explanation of the three stages; second, the general explanation of the abandonment of hindrances.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the three stages, the text is divided into three sections:
The first is the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
This section is further divided into two parts;
first, the initial part clarifies the Immovable Stage.
Sūtra:

“The Bodhisattva Immovable, King of the Second Dhyāna, has attained a body of transformation and is eternally sovereign; he is able, within millions of lands as numerous as motes of dust, to manifest according to the forms and types [of beings] to transform sentient beings.”
The commentary states:
This clarifies "middle patience.
It designates the name of the stage, clarifying the dwelling place of the King and clarifying the attainment of the victorious body.

Regarding "ever-sovereign," both the manifested marks and the lands are entirely sovereign, because it is clarified that the realms of those to be transformed are transformed according to their respective types.
This is the second section, clarifying "ever-immovable."
Sūtra:
"He fully knows the immeasurable kalpas of the three periods of time, remaining forever unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Explanation:
"Thoroughly knowing the three periods of time" means that clear wisdom illuminates them.
"Immeasurable eons" means knowing that both the past and future periods are immeasurable.

"Regarding the primary truth" means that although the Bodhisattvas of this stage constantly realize suchness, they remain ever unmoving as they maintain the simultaneous manifestation of both the ultimate and the conventional truths.
From here, the second stage, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), is elucidated.
The Sūtra states:

"The Bodhisattva of Excellent Intelligence is a king of the third dhyāna; he can manifest [himself] simultaneously throughout a thousand Ganges-sands of worlds. He constantly dwells in the practice of unconditioned emptiness and quiescence, and realizes the Buddha-treasuries as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in a single thought-moment."
The commentary states:
This clarifies the stage of "Superior Patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti).
It designates the name of the ground to clarify the dwelling place of the King, the realm of those to be transformed, and the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Wisdom constantly realizes suchness, for the ultimate and the conventional are equal, being both empty and quiescent.
"The Buddha-treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" clarifies the possession of merit;

the teachings flowing from the various Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this stage of Bodhisattva is able to comprehend through the four types of unimpeded knowledge within a single thought-moment.
From here begins the third [section], clarifying the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
This is divided into two parts;
first, the initial section clarifies the Dharma-Cloud Stage.
Sūtra:

“The Bodhisattva Dharmamegha, King of the Fourth Dhyāna, transforms sentient beings across billions of Ganges-sands of lands; having first entered the diamond-like samādhi of total realization, he has forever transcended twenty-nine births.”
The commentary states:
This refers to the lowest grade within the patience of cessation (*kṣānti*).
It designates the name of the stage to clarify the dwelling place of the King and the realm of those he transforms.
"Beginning with the entry into the Vajra" refers to the supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) at the end.
"Beginning" means the initial moment; "entry" means realization.

At the final moment of mind in this stage, the Vajra-samādhi arises; through the first uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the principle is realized and manifests before one. Since the obstacles of affliction are forever eliminated and illuminating understanding is perfected, it is called "all-encompassing comprehension."

This stage of perfect enlightenment is subsumed within the Dharma-cloud Stage (Dharmameghā-bhūmi); it is divided into two halves, upper and lower, in order to manifest the preceding and succeeding stages.
The manner in which one transcends and is born [into these stages] is fully explained in the text.
From this, the second section clarifies the inferior grade of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).
The Sūtra states:
"Within the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*), the observation of the inferior grade is a single revolution of wondrous awakening, which is peerless."
The commentary states:
"To mention the name 'patience' (kṣānti) is to clarify the contemplation of the lower patience.
To speak of 'one turn' is to distinguish the stage of patience."

When this state of immediate succession (ānantarya) transforms into liberation, it is called "one turning" (*ekāvartana*), which is precisely what is termed "wondrous enlightenment" (*samyaksaṃbodhi*); thus the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected. Regarding the term "unequaled" (*asama*):

if the preceding moment is viewed from the perspective of cause toward fruit, it is called "unequaled"; however, upon reaching the stage of liberation, where the paths of all Buddhas are equal, it is called "equal. This is because the current stage of lower patience (*kṣānti*) clarifies that such a transformation is imminent.
From this, the second section generally clarifies the severing of hindrances.
The Sūtra states:

"The Immovable, Good Wisdom, and Dharma Cloud stages eliminate all prior habitual tendencies of ignorance; the habitual tendencies of ignorance and their corresponding consciousnesses cease to function together, as the principles of the two truths are perfected and nothing remains unexhausted."
The commentary states:
"Referring to the three preceding stages above.
'Eliminating all prior habitual tendencies of ignorance' refers to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)."

Apart from the specific portions of the obstructions of form and mind that were eliminated in each of the preceding seven stages, the remaining subtle obstructions are severed individually within these three stages.

Regarding the statement that "the habitual tendencies of ignorance and the evolving consciousness function together": this refers to the seeds of the afflictive obstructions to be abandoned through cultivation, as well as the subtle seeds of the ignorance associated with the seventh consciousness; because they persist together with the evolving consciousness until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), they are said to "function together."
Furthermore, as in the *Awakening of Faith*, fundamental ignorance coexists with the karmic consciousness; how then can it be said that they are abandoned through transformation?

Regarding the statement that "the principle of the two truths is perfect and exhaustive," this clarifies that at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyagjñāna*), the illumination and understanding are perfectly integrated in essence, such that there is nothing among the abandoned or discarded that is not fully exhausted.
From here, one and a half lines clarify the stage of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This section is divided into two parts;
first, the initial part clarifies the perfection of perfect enlightenment.

In Sanskrit it is called *sambodhi*, which here means "Right Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the unsurpassed awakening.
As for the term "signless" (*animitta*), it refers to the fact that both the subject that realizes and the object realized are devoid of signs.
Regarding "pervading the entire dharma-realm": each and every one of the merits, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is boundless; even the tip of a single hair pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Regarding "the exhaustion of thirty births": this refers to transcending the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because those births have been exhausted.
"Wisdom is perfectly bright" means that wisdom has reached its ultimate perfection.
From this second point, it clarifies that the Buddha is endowed with virtues.
The Sūtra says:

“Quiescent illumination and unconditionedness are true liberation; the manifestation of great compassion is peerless. Tranquil and unmoving, eternally secure, its radiance shines everywhere yet has nothing upon which to shine.”
The commentary states:
"Quiescent illumination" clarifies that the perfection of the merit of wisdom has been attained.
"Unconditioned true liberation" clarifies that the perfection of the merit of cessation has been attained.
"The manifestation of great compassion" clarifies the perfection of the virtue of grace.
"Having no equal" clarifies that the aforementioned three virtues are all without peer.
"Serene and unmoving" reveals the virtue of grace.

By virtue of the Buddha’s great compassion and the power of his vows to benefit others, he manifests various types of bodies, both large and small; because he moves while remaining eternally quiescent, he is said to be "serenely still," and though he displays coming and going, his essence is eternally unmoving.
"Peaceful and secure" refers to the manifestation of transformation.
For instance, when he ate horse fodder or manifested the shedding of blood, he never wavered; he was always peaceful and secure.
"The light shines everywhere" means that the essence of his benevolent virtue is like a pure maṇi jewel; its substance pervades the Dharma-realm, shining yet without shining.
The second major section concludes the preceding discussion of cause and effect.
The Sūtra states:
"Those of the Three Worthies and Ten Sages dwell in the retribution of their fruits; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land."
"All sentient beings abide for a time, yet upon ascending the Vajra Ground, they are eternally immovable.
The commentary states:
"The three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages abiding in retribution" is explained in terms of persons.
Regarding the two types of birth and death—fragmentary and transformational—whether it be the body or the land, one dwells in the retribution of results because they are induced by causes.
As for the statement that "only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land," the Tathāgata is also called the Unsurpassed Awakened One, for wherever his body resides is itself a pure land.
"All sentient beings abide only temporarily" clarifies this in terms of phenomena.

From the stage prior to Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), whether one is a worthy one (ārya) or a noble one (ārya), conditioned existence arises and ceases, not abiding for even a single moment; even if one realizes Suchness (tathatā), it is likewise only a temporary abiding.
Regarding the statement that "ascending the Vajra-ground, one is eternally immovable," there are two meanings. Some say:
In the stage of the Buddha’s true liberation, wisdom constantly realizes suchness (*tathatā*); because suchness and wisdom are equal, it is called "immovable."
Because they are both termed "constant" (*nitya*) due to their unceasing continuity. Some say:
after the Buddha-fruit’s adamantine concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), one realizes the source of quiescence; body and wisdom are profoundly still and eternally unmoving.
From here, the second section consists of two and a half lines praising the Buddha’s profound compassion.
This is divided into three parts;
first, the initial section provides a general praise of the depth of his compassion.
Sūtra:
"The Tathāgata’s virtues of the three karmas are immeasurable; he extends equal compassion to all sentient beings.
Explanation:
This is a general praise for the immeasurable virtue of the three karmas.
The phrase "compassionately regarding all sentient beings equally" specifically praises the profundity of his compassion.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion and pity are impartial; he reveals the Unsurpassed Vehicle according to their respective dispositions, precisely because his true compassion is profound.
From here, the second section separately praises the three karmas.
The Sūtra says:

"The Dharma King, the unsurpassed tree among men, universally shades the great assembly with immeasurable light; his mouth constantly preaches the Dharma, never without meaning, while his mind and wisdom are in tranquil extinction, illuminating without an object."
The commentary states:
"The 'tree among men' is an illustration used for clarification.
It praises the Buddha’s bodily karma (*kāyakarman*): its shade removes the afflictions of attachment, and its light is able to destroy darkness."
"One whose mouth constantly preaches the Dharma" refers to the praise of vocal karma.
"Preaching" is sound; it is as profound as thunder and possesses the Brahma-voice.

"Not being without meaning" means that while non-Buddhists and ordinary beings have words but no meaning, and the followers of the Two Vehicles are narrow and inferior, and Bodhisattvas are not yet perfected, only what is spoken by the Buddha possesses both words and meaning, all of which are complete and perfect.
"The mind and intellect are quiescent" praises right wisdom;
for when wisdom merges with ultimate truth, it is eternally quiescent.
"Illumination without an object" praises its functional activity.
The profound reality gives rise to transformation, yet all is devoid of marks; it illuminates without illumination and transforms without transformation.
From this, the third section praises and explains the profound.
Scripture:
“The Lion among Men has expounded this profound and unprecedented White Dharma; all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges tremble, and the great assembly rejoices, all receiving its benefit.”
The commentary states:
"The Lion among Men" refers to the fact that when a lion roars, all other beasts cower; likewise, when the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma, the clouds of all obstacles vanish—hence this metaphor.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of expounding," this praises the five patiences (*kṣānti*).

As for "profound" and so forth: because the two vehicles cannot fathom them, they are called "profound"; because they have been difficult to hear throughout vast eons and are unprecedented, they are so described.
"Equal to the sands of the Ganges" refers to how, through the power of the Dharma, one hears what has never been heard before, causing lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to all tremble.
"The great assembly" refers to how the great assembly hears the Dharma, attains understanding, and rejoices; whether ordinary beings or sages, all receive its benefit.
Possessing these manifold virtues, he is praised for the profundity of his compassion.
Thirdly, regarding why he is specifically praised within the demonstration of the path: it is because the benefit and happiness of the subsequent instructions and guidance are vast.
This concludes the third section: the summary praise and respectful salutation.
Sūtra:
“The World-Honored One has excellently expounded upon the fourteen kings; therefore, I now prostrate with my head at his feet.
Explanation:
The meaning is easy to understand; this concludes the section of praise.
From here begins the third [section]: the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma.
The Sūtra says:

At that time, a great assembly as numerous as the sands of ten million billion Ganges Rivers, having heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and King Prasenajit discourse upon the immeasurable merits of the fourteen kinds of patience (*kṣānti*), attained the great benefit of the Dharma; through hearing the Dharma, they awakened to its meaning and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), entering the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The commentary states:
"The patience of non-arising" refers, according to its application, to the patience of non-arising prior to the various stages (bhūmi).
"Entering the state of certainty" refers specifically to the first stage (bhūmi).

Regarding the difference between the verses and the prose: in the prose, the practice of the various forms of patience increases one's own benefit, while in the verses, the transformation into a king excels in benefiting others; thus, the verses synthesize these two preceding points, which constitutes their distinction.
From this third stage, the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), there are three divisions:
first, a seal-like summary of what has been taught; second, the objects and wisdom of the stage of Patience; and third, a praise of the profound virtue of Patience.
Regarding what was explained in the first seal, it is divided into four parts;
first, the initial section clarifies the causes of the past.
The Sūtra states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"This King Prasenajit was already a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage during the Dharma of King Dragon-Radiance (Nāgaprabhāsa) ten thousand kalpas ago, while I was a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage."
The commentary states:
This citation clarifies "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) from the perspective of past causes.
From this point, the second section clarifies the present verse of praise.
Sūtra:
"Now, before me, he lets out a great lion’s roar.
Explanation:
Having praised [the Buddha] before him, he attained the definitive teaching.
From this follows the third seal of approval for what was spoken.
Sūtra:
"It is so, it is so. As you have said, the attainment of the true meaning is inconceivable.
The commentary states:

Regarding the repeated statement "thus" (*evam*): as you have said, if the seal that expresses the text attains the true meaning, then it is the seal of the meaning expressed; for this reason, it is stated repeatedly as "thus, thus."
Regarding "inconceivable," it praises the phrasing and meaning as being beyond the path of mind and speech;
from this fourth point onward, only a Buddha can know it.
Sūtra:
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas know this matter.
The commentary states:

"Only Buddhas," and so forth, because the bodhisattvas' cultivation and realization of the various patiences (*kṣānti*) are not yet perfected; even if they were later [to attain them], they would all be partial, just as before.
Only the Buddhas possess a Buddha-way that is uniform; because their realization, understanding, and patience are perfected, they know all things exhaustively.
This is the second section: the objects and wisdom of the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).
Within this, there are three parts:
First, the indication that patience is immeasurable; second, the general inquiry; third, the detailed explanation.
First, regarding the initial indication that patience is immeasurable, the Sūtra says:
“Good son! These fourteen kinds of patience—the Dharma-body of all Buddhas and the practices of all Bodhisattvas—are inconceivable and immeasurable.”
The commentary states:

In the preceding prose section, the Buddha spoke of the ten kings; subsequently, in the verse section, he specifically praises patience (*kṣānti*). This fully elucidates both the objective realm and the wisdom of patience, as well as its causes and fruits.
"These fourteen kinds of patience" refers back to the preceding text.
"The Dharma-body of all Buddhas" means that both the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) are the Dharma-body.
"The practices of all Bodhisattvas" refers to all practices prior to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Regarding "inconceivable" and so forth: it is that which the mind cannot conceive and the mouth cannot discuss; because it transcends the sphere of calculation and measurement, it is said to be "unfathomable.
This clarifies that both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely upon this patience (*kṣānti*); as for the nature and characteristics of this patience, they are beyond both conception and calculation.
From this point, the second section consists of general inquiries.
The Sūtra says:
"For what reason?"
The commentary states:
For what reason do all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely on the fourteen types of patience (*kṣānti*) that are inconceivable?
This is the third section, which provides a detailed analysis and explanation.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, a detailed explanation of the object and the wisdom; second, an explanation that resolves the difficulty regarding their immeasurability.
Within the first part, the explanation of the object and wisdom, there are further two subdivisions:
First, the elucidation of the Buddha’s realm and wisdom; second, the elucidation of the Bodhisattvas’ realm and wisdom.
Regarding the first—the Buddha’s realm and wisdom—it is divided into three parts:
first, indicating the Buddha’s transformation, birth, and cessation; second, explaining the absence of birth, transformation, and cessation; third, concluding that it is like empty space.
Furthermore, first, the sūtra marks the Buddha’s birth, transformation, and extinction:
"All Buddhas are born within the *prajñāpāramitā*, transform within the *prajñāpāramitā*, and extinguish within the *prajñāpāramitā*."
The commentary states:
In the *prajñā* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there is no arising or ceasing.

Yet, as the manifested forms of the Buddhas respond perfectly throughout the ten directions, they manifest within this *prajñā* the appearance of birth and cessation; that is, their birth in the royal palace, their turning of the wheel of Dharma, and their final passing away at the twin śāla trees—these are precisely those events.
From this point, the second [section] explains that there is no arising or ceasing of beings;
herein, there are again two parts.
First, the initial part explains the absence of arising and so forth.
Sūtra:
“In reality, all Buddhas are born where there is no birth, transform where there is no transformation, and pass away where there is no passing away.
Explanation:

This means that the essence of all Buddhas is pervasive and their marks are perfect; though they move, they are eternally quiescent, and thus there is no arising, transformation, birth, or extinction.
From this follows the second [point]: both object and wisdom are quiescent.
The Sūtra says:
"First and without a second, neither with marks nor without marks, without self and without other, without coming and without going.
The commentary states:
"The term 'first' refers to its superiority, as there is nothing equal to it."
To say it is "without duality" means that wisdom is not different [from its object].
To say it is "not characterized by marks" means it does not share the same nature as material forms.
To say it is "not without marks" means it is not like a rabbit's horn.

Regarding "neither self nor other": although the manifested transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) exhibit distinctions of superiority and inferiority, they are no different from the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*) in being devoid of self and other.
Regarding "neither coming nor going": while transformations manifest to accord with sentient beings, appearing to come and go, their essence is eternally unmoving and thus free from coming and going.
From this, the third summary is "like space.
The Sūtra says:
"Because it is like space."
The commentary states:
Stillness does not contradict movement; while moving, one is always quiescent. Thus, stillness is realized within movement, for it is like empty space.
Following this, the second section clarifies the objective realm and wisdom of the Bodhisattva.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, observing emptiness through the object; second, observing emptiness through wisdom.
Within the first part, observing emptiness through the object, the text is further divided into two sections.
First is the contemplation of emptiness through specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and second is the contemplation of emptiness through general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

Within the first, the section on specific characteristics, the text is divided into two parts: first, the contemplation of emptiness regarding phenomena (*dharma*), and second, the contemplation of emptiness regarding sensation (*vedanā*).
Within the first section on the Dharma, the text is further divided into three parts;
first, the initial point designates the absence of arising and ceasing.
The Sūtra states:
"Good son! The nature of all sentient beings is without arising or ceasing.
Explanation:
This reveals the reliance upon the Truth (tathatā).
"All sentient beings" refers universally to all beings, both those who transform and those who are transformed.
The intrinsic nature and essence of the aggregates and so forth are precisely suchness (tathatā), because they are without arising or ceasing.
From this second point, it clarifies that phenomena are not real.
The Sūtra states:

"Because all phenomena arise through the gathering of illusions and transformations, the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) neither combine nor disperse."
The commentary states:
This means that since beginningless time, one has been deluded regarding one’s own true nature and moved by phenomenal marks; thus, one is made to realize the illusory nature [of things].
As for "all phenomena arising through the collection of illusions," this refers to the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The coming together of the five aggregates is called "arising"; this has no substantial reality, existing as a magical illusion.
The aggregates, bases, and elements clarify the nature of illusory phenomena.
To say there is no "coming together" means that the aggregates arise from conditions, and since those conditions are empty of intrinsic nature, there is no coming together.
Regarding the statement "there is no dispersion": because it is a temporary manifestation resulting from the provisional gathering of various conditions, it is not dispersed.
This concludes the third section, which clarifies the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).
The Sūtra says:
"Phenomena are identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), for they are quiescent and empty.
The commentary states:
"The 'phenomena' mentioned above refer to the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth."
That which shares the same dharma-nature is identical to the nature of true thusness (*tathatā*).
Nature and appearance support one another; their substance is not separate. To realize that appearance is itself nature is because it is quiescently empty.
From this second [section], one then practices the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This is divided into three parts:
first, the purity of essential nature; second, clarifying that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are unreal; and third, a summary concluding with the clarification of emptiness.
Furthermore, first is the indication of the purity of intrinsic nature.
The Sūtra states:
"All sentient beings are pure by their very nature."
The commentary states: This indicates that the true nature (*dharmatā*) of sentient beings is pure.

As for its distinction from what preceded: the former clarifies that the essence of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is devoid of arising and ceasing; this clarifies that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of their activity is pure. Furthermore, they differ in that the former concerns the fruit and the latter the cause, the former the phenomenon (*dharma*) and the latter the recipient (*vedaka*), and the former suffering (*duḥkha*) and the latter its origin (*samudaya*). Thus, these two are distinct.
From this point, the second section clarifies that formations (*saṃskāra*) are unreal.
This text is further divided into two parts;
first, the initial section clarifies that formations are unreal.
Sūtra:
“All conditioned phenomena that are performed are neither bound nor liberated; they are neither cause nor effect, yet not without cause or effect.
Explanation:
This clarifies the activity of karma.

Regarding "the various formations" (*saṃskāra*): "various" means manifold; "formations" refers to the act of constructing. Based on body, speech, and mind, one constructs the karmic actions of the six destinies—whether wholesome or defiled—and these are termed "various formations."
Regarding "neither bound nor liberated": it is because one is moved by delusion and bound by afflictions that one seeks liberation from those fetters; thus, there is bondage and liberation.
But when one realizes that the essence is itself the Truth and has been fundamentally without bondage from the beginning, who would further seek liberation?
This is precisely neither bondage nor liberation.

That which is neither cause nor effect refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are seen as existent due to delusion; yet their delusive intrinsic nature is empty, and thus they are neither cause nor effect.

"It is not that cause and effect do not exist" means that, failing to realize that the self-nature is but a drifting and racing of false conceptualization, one experiences results conditioned by causes, which exist like an illusion.
From this, the second point clarifies that experience is unreal.
Sūtra:
“All painful sensations, the activities of afflictions and the objects of knowledge, the mark of self, the mark of person, and the knower, seer, and receiver.
Commentary:
This clarifies the experience of delusion.

Regarding the phrase "all sufferings," when discussed in general terms across the three realms, there are three types of suffering; because these three sufferings are not identical, they are termed "all.

Regarding the phrase "the practice of feeling" (*vedanā-saṃskāra*): "feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to reception, having as its nature the objective aspects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neither; thus it is called the "practice of feeling."
Its function is to give rise to craving toward objects that have been experienced, whether wholesome or defiled; its mode of activity consists in experiencing those objects as they are performed.
As for the term "affliction" (*kleśa*), it means being weary, fatigued, and disturbed, because it afflicts all states of existence (*bhava*).
Regarding the term "objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*): they obstruct wisdom from arising because they hinder what is to be known; thus, they are the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
As for "the signs of self" (*ātma-ādi*) and so forth, these have already been explained as above.
The obstacles arise based on grasping; the obstacles are broad while grasping is narrow. Because they give rise to both types of obstacles, they are explained separately.
This is the third section, which concludes by clarifying emptiness.
Sūtra:
"All things are empty. Explanation:
This clarifies that from the performed actions up to the recipient, all exist by flowing according to deluded mental states; since they all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all things are empty.
From here follows the second section, the general contemplation of emptiness.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the designation of the emptiness of the objective sphere; second, the explanation of the emptiness of the objective sphere; and third, the conclusion that it is like empty space.
Furthermore, first, the emptiness of the objective realm is indicated.
The Sūtra says:
"The objective realm of dharmas is empty."
The commentary states:

Regarding the "sphere of phenomena" (*dharmaviṣaya*), among the various conditioned phenomena and feelings produced by the aforementioned aggregates and so forth—namely, the three natures, the six destinies, and the Three Jewels—all are termed "phenomena" because they are marked as being equally empty.
From here begins the second [section], the explanation of the emptiness of the objective sphere (*ālambana-śūnyatā*).
This is divided into three parts;
first, the initial section clarifies the emptiness of the three natures (*trisvabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Sūtra:
“Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness do not conform to inversion; they do not conform to illusion.
Explanation:
"Emptiness" refers to the emptiness of delusive inversions.
"Signlessness" refers to the signlessness of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Actionlessness" refers to the unreality of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), as they are not produced by themselves.
"Not conforming to perversions" means that the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty, as there is nothing to conform to.
"Not conforming to illusions" means that appearances have no self-nature, for their substance is empty and quiescent.
From this, the second section clarifies signless emptiness (*animitta-śūnyatā*).
The Sūtra says:
"There is no characteristic of the six destinies, no characteristic of the four modes of birth, no characteristic of the noble ones, and no characteristic of the Three Jewels."
The commentary states:
"The destinies and births are indeterminate in their three natures; they lack intrinsic nature because they are illuminated as emptiness.
'There are no noble ones' means that the noble ones of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages lack intrinsic nature."

Regarding "the absence of the Three Jewels": this refers to the two types of the Three Jewels—the distinct characteristics and the sustaining [relics]—because while the Buddha-body manifests in appearance, all else lacks intrinsic nature; having realized their lack of substantial reality, they are all without marks.
From this, the third summary is "like space.
The Sūtra says:
"Because it is like space."
The commentary states:
"Illuminating that objects are empty and quiescent, because they are like space.
This second point refers to the contemplation of emptiness through wisdom (*jñāna*).
This section is divided into three parts.
First, "The Illumination of Emptiness by the Wisdom of Clear Intelligence.
Scripture states:
“Good son! The profound *prajñā* is without knowing and without seeing; it does not function and does not take objects; it neither abandons nor receives.
Explanation:
"Profound prajñā" refers to right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
As for the statement "there is no knowing":
Because it is non-conceptual,
it is said to be "without seeing";
because it is without seeking, it is "without viewing."
"Words do not function" means that wisdom is darkened [unified] with the Truth.
"Words do not take objects as their conditions" means:
Because it lacks the characteristic of having an object (*ālambana*),
it is said to be "not abandoned": that is,
because it cannot be easily detached from.
Regarding the term "non-appropriation" (anupātta): it means there is no experiencing or reception [of sensation].
These are the six meanings:
This is the perfect wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
Furthermore, another interpretation is:
there is nothing that is not known; though knowing, there is no [discursive] knowing.
There is nothing that is not seen, yet seeing is without seeing.
This continues through the sixth point, where there is nothing that is not received, yet receiving is without receiving.
These latter six meanings encompass both the ultimate and the conventional truths.

Subsequently, regarding these six: "practice" refers to the myriad practices; "conditions" refers to principle and phenomena; "giving" refers to the giving of wealth and Dharma, or the great relinquishment (*mahātyāga*); and "reception" refers to the unchanging nature of both the ultimate and conventional truths.
Realizing the ultimate truth and penetrating the conventional, one attains non-abiding.
From this, secondly, the aspect of non-apprehension is clarified.
Scripture states:
"Abiding correctly in observation, there is illumination without the appearance of signs.
The commentary states:
Non-conceptual wisdom abides correctly in manifestation; it illuminates yet does not illuminate, because it does not dwell upon signs.
From this, the third [section] concludes by clarifying that wisdom is empty,
as the Sūtra states: "Those who practice this path are like empty space."
The commentary states:
Those who practice this path—namely, the various bodhisattvas—rely upon this to realize and cultivate [the truth], wherein both object and wisdom are quiescent, like empty space.
Furthermore, to establish a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) for those who do not know how to eliminate the appearance of signs (*nimitta*) yet claim to possess correct understanding, it is said:
Contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*) is the principle of existence; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the markless appearance (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*) are the principles that constitute the method.
The union of these principles and the principle of existence constitutes the fundamental tenet (*siddhānta*).
Because they are without cognition and without vision, the three are differentiated yet unified as the causal dharma.
"Like space"—this is the illustrative dharma (*dṛṣṭāntadharma*).

If that were so, it would accord with the tenets of the Buddha's disciples; however, the masters of the Hīnayāna schools would each incur a fault regarding one or another of the logical reasons (*hetu*).
Whether there is emptiness or no emptiness, the analogy commits the fallacy of both being unestablished;
briefly, there are four faults.

If [the argument] is directed against non-Buddhists, since their own tenets distinguish specific entities, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not universally established (*aprasiddha*); this constitutes the fallacy of "one of the two being unestablished" (*anyatarāsiddha*), as they do not accept this [qualification].
Regarding the absence of knowledge and vision, etc., the grasping of that "non-conceptual" state is not established here.
This is like the debate between those who assert emptiness and those who deny it; whether both exist or both do not exist, neither pair is established, as there are briefly six fallacies.

Consequently, throughout the subsequent sections clarifying the objects and wisdom of patience (*kṣānti*), there are numerous inferential arguments (*anumāna*) in each passage; all are free from fault and capable of generating correct understanding. Furthermore, within the sphere of the Bodhisattva’s objective knowledge (*jñeya-jñāna*), these [four truths] likewise correspond respectively to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

This section is divided into two parts:
First, the immeasurability is explained, and finally, the immeasurability is concluded.

Sūtra:
“The characteristics of dharmas are thus: the mind that apprehends something and the mind that does not apprehend anything are both unapprehendable.
Explanation:
That the characteristics of dharmas are thus refers to the wisdom regarding the preceding objects.
"The mind that has something to attain" is the mind that grasps at signs.
"The mind that has nothing to attain" is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
That "all are unobtainable" means that the mind of attainment previously held is unobtainable because it is false;
the wisdom of non-attainment subsequently realized is unobtainable because it is true.
Even if one has not yet attained direct realization, the semblance of suchness as an object-condition is likewise unobtainable.
This constitutes the initial heading, the subsequent enumeration, and the final summary within the four propositions.
From here begins the second section: the explanation of neither identity nor difference.
The Sūtra states:

"Therefore, Prajñā is neither identical to the five aggregates nor separate from the five aggregates; it is neither identical to sentient beings nor separate from sentient beings; it is neither identical to objects of perception nor separate from objects of perception; it is neither identical to practice and understanding nor separate from practice and understanding."
The commentary states:
The four preceding passages explain that while their essence is entirely *prajñā*, they differ in terms of liberation and bondage due to the mind’s delusion or enlightenment.
Therefore, *prajñā* is the designated dharma that can be explained.
It is not identical to the five aggregates, for they exist as illusory fabrications.
Since this is not illusory fabrication, it is therefore "not" [the aggregates].
It is not separate from the five aggregates, for the reality-mark (dharmatā) is equal in essence and pervades all things; thus, it is not separate.
This explains what was stated above: "All phenomena exist as illusory transformations through their aggregation.
It is not identical to sentient beings; because sentient beings are subject to delusion and inversion, whereas this is not deluded or inverted, it is therefore not identical to them.
It cannot be known apart from [the mind].
This explains the various conditioned activities performed by sentient beings.
That it is not identical to the objective realm means that the aforementioned realms are false because they are not clearly understood.
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is not false; therefore, it is "not.
This "not" is not something separate from what can be known.
This explains the subsequent passage concerning the sphere of experience (*viṣaya*).

"Neither identical with nor separate from practice and understanding": practice and understanding are precisely the wisdom of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). If one abides in signs, it is said to be "neither identical"; if there is no conceptual differentiation, it is said to be "not separate."
By means of the explanation regarding "contemplation," it is known that cessation, realization, and cultivation are the four distinct [aspects].
From this, thirdly, there is the general explanation of the immeasurable.
The Sūtra says:
"Such characteristics as these are inconceivable.
The commentary states:
These aforementioned natures and characteristics of the forbearance of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot be conceived or measured; their virtues transcend all calculation and thought.
From this point, the second section clarifies the "Inconceivable Summation.
This is divided into three parts;
first, the initial summation of the bodhisattva practices.
Sūtra:
"Therefore, all practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are practiced within them before reaching their ultimate consummation.
Commentary:
This concludes the various practices of the bodhisattvas mentioned above.
The phrase "therefore" serves as a term to conclude what has preceded.
The term "all" refers to all bodhisattvas, both those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those who have attained them.
From the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the attainment of Buddhahood, one practices entirely within the sphere of contemplation (*cintā*).

Although the essential nature of patience (*kṣānti*) is devoid of distinctions between the holy and the ordinary, it is by relying on patience that cultivation is distinguished; therefore, this clarifies the Bodhisattva.
From this second point, the transformation of all Buddhas is summarized.
The Sūtra states:
"All Buddhas know that [all things] are like illusions and transformations; having attained the mark of non-abiding, they manifest transformations therein."
The commentary states:
"All Buddhas" refers here to the Dharma-body of all Buddhas mentioned in the heading.
"Knowing them to be like illusions and transformations" means knowing that the beings thus transformed are like illusions and lack substantial reality.
If one were not reached by the teaching, there would be no liberation from the bonds of illusion;

therefore, he manifests transformation. As for those who have attained the mark of non-abiding: while all ordinary beings delight in dwelling within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the noble ones of the two vehicles delight in dwelling in *nirvāṇa*, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained the path of non-abiding and are constantly supported by great compassion and great wisdom. Consequently, they do not abide in either birth-and-death or *nirvāṇa*. Whether their bodies appear different or identical, they constantly bring about benefit and joy.
Furthermore, those who undergo transformation therein are subsumed under the realms, destinies, noble ones, and patiences, and because they undergo transformation therein.
From this, thirdly, the patience that is difficult to measure is concluded.
Sūtra:
"Therefore, the fourteen patiences are inconceivable.
The commentary says:
This is a summary.

However, according to the distinction made between the exposition and the conclusion within the headings, the exposition follows what comes later while the conclusion refers back to what precedes it; thus, the text deviates from its sequential order.
Furthermore, within the conclusions, the persons also deviate from their sequence: the headings are based on cause and fruit, whereas the conclusions rely on practice and transformation.
These two are distinct.
From here begins the third section, which praises the profundity of the virtue of patience (*kṣānti*).
This is divided into three parts:
First, the indication that the benefit is vast; second, the illustration that it is immeasurable; third, the praise by all Buddhas.
First, regarding the initial indication that the benefit is vast, the Sūtra says:
“Good son! This treasury of merit that you have now described provides great benefit for all sentient beings.
Explanation:
It is praised that the patience thus explained is a treasury of merit, for it gives rise to hearing, reflection, and so forth, thereby bringing extensive benefit and happiness.
Following this, the second metaphor describes its immeasurability.
The Sūtra says:

"Even if Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, were to speak of these merits, they would constitute but a hundred-thousand-billionth part of them, like a single drop in the ocean.
The commentary states:
"This explains that the enlightened virtue is vast."
"Even if there were as many as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers" clarifies their great number.
"Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages" clarifies their excellence; among all bodhisattvas, those of the Ten Stages are the most excellent.
To speak of these merits refers to the merit of patience (*kṣānti*).
The phrase "a hundred thousand *koṭis* of parts" is used as a metaphor to clarify this.

It means that when the virtue of patience is perfected, its magnitude is equal to the *dharmadhātu*, like the great ocean; yet even the praises spoken throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are but a single drop within those hundred thousand *koṭis* of parts.
If that is so, since the realization attained by Vīrasena was at most only that of the tenth bhūmi, why is his praise of the tenth bhūmi inferior?
Answer:
Vīrasena’s teaching on patience is identical to the Buddha’s teaching, and his praise of the merit of patience is likewise as previously stated—like a single drop [of water].
Third, regarding the praise by all Buddhas, the Sūtra states:

“The Buddhas of the three periods of time know this as it truly is; all worthy ones and sages alike offer their praise. Therefore, I shall now briefly describe a small portion of the merits thus taught.”
The commentary states:

All the merits possessed by these fourteen patiences are known as they truly are by the Buddhas of the three periods of time; all bodhisattvas, whether ordinary or noble, who practice in reliance upon these patiences, universally praise them.

Regarding the phrase "therefore, equally," if the Buddha were to explain it in full detail, there would be fear that confusion and transgression might arise; therefore, the Buddha briefly describes only a small portion of its merits.
From this point on is the fourth section: the common practice of all Buddhas.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, the common practice of all Buddhas; second, the clarification of the arising of pure faith.
Within the first section on common practice, the text is further divided into two parts:
The first part concerns the common cultivation throughout the three periods of time, while the latter clarifies what must necessarily be cultivated.
