first, the common cultivation regarding the past and present.
Sūtra: “Good son!
These fourteen patiences are what all bodhisattvas of the past and present in the worlds of the ten directions have practiced.”
The commentary states:
This explains that the gate of patience is cultivated by Bodhisattvas in common.
From this second point onward, it clarifies the Buddha’s manifestation.
Sūtra:
"That which is revealed by all Buddhas. Commentary:
This explains that they speak in agreement.
From here, the third section clarifies the future collectively.
The Sūtra says:
"Future Buddhas, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will also be like this.
The commentary states:
This is an analogy for those of the past and present.
From this point, the second section clarifies that one must necessarily practice;
herein it is divided into three parts.
First, the initial part clarifies that one must necessarily practice.
Sūtra:
"If a Buddha or Bodhisattva were to attain all-knowledge without entering through this gate, such a thing is impossible.
Explanation:
Regarding the phrase "not dependent," "dependent" (you) means cause or basis; it carries the sense of "by means of.

If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were not dependent upon patience (*kṣānti*), and could not enter this gate to attain the fruit of Buddhahood and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), such a thing would be impossible.
From this, the second [section] investigates the reason why.
The Sūtra asks:
“For what reason?”
The commentary states:
Why is it that one who does not cultivate patience does not attain Buddhahood?
This is the third [section], which explains the lack of basis [for such a claim].
Sūtra:
“Because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have no divergent paths.
Explanation:
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not attain Buddhahood by relying on the gradual cultivation and realization of the gates of patience (*kṣānti*), nor by any other path;
from this second point, the arising of pure faith (*śraddhā*) is clarified.
This section is divided into two parts.
First, regarding the initial point, the clear exposition on transcending kalpas,
the Sūtra states:

“If there is a person who, upon hearing of these—namely, the patience of abiding, the patience of practice, the patience of dedication, the patience of joy, the patience of freedom from defilement, the patience of radiant light, the patience of flaming wisdom, the patience of difficult victory, the patience of manifestation, the patience of far-reaching travel, the patience of immovability, the patience of excellent wisdom, the patience of the Dharma-cloud, and the patience of perfect enlightenment—is able to give rise to even a single thought of pure faith, that person shall transcend all hardships and sufferings of hundreds, thousands, and immeasurable, boundless *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas, and shall not be born in the evil realms.”
The commentary states:

Throughout the long kalpas of birth and death, there is no way to hear this name. If one should happen to hear it and give rise to neither doubt nor slander, but instead produce deep pure faith—even if it is as little as a single thought of pure faith—such a person will immediately transcend hundreds of thousands [of kalpas], meaning they will transcend the various sufferings and eight difficulties of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and will not be born in the evil realms.
How much more so for one who upholds, recites, and studies it for a long time, giving rise to hearing, reflection, and cultivation—how could they fail to transcend?
From this, secondly, the attainment of bodhi is elucidated.
Sūtra:
"Before long, one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The commentary explains:
By virtue of the aforementioned pure faith, not only does one transcend suffering, but one shall also attain *bodhi* before long.
From here begins the third section, the Practice of the Great Assembly.
This is divided into three parts;
first, we shall briefly identify those who hear the Dharma.
Sūtra:
At that time, ten billion Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas named Ākāśagarbha, together with an immeasurable and incalculable multitude of those who had gathered, were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
The commentary states:

At the time of hearing and accepting [the teaching], those who share the name "Bodhisattva" together with the great assembly—namely, the great assembly enumerated in the "Introductory Chapter"—all leaped for joy.
From this second section, the vision of all Buddhas is clarified.
The Sūtra says:

"By virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they universally behold the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, each expounding the fourteen kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) at their respective sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), no different from what our World-Honored One has taught."
The commentary states:
Because they have heard the Dharma and received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they immediately see the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.

Regarding the phrase "each at their respective sites of enlightenment," it means that all Buddhas, each residing in the site of enlightenment in their own land, preach the fourteen kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) within the ocean-like assemblies.

Now, what the World-Honored One has taught is without difference; it expresses the identity of the speaker and expresses the identity of the teaching, so that through the majestic power of the Dharma, one attains identity in hearing and seeing.

As in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where Bodhisattva Dharmamati expounds the Ten Abodes, Bodhisattva Guṇakara expounds the Ten Practices, Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja expounds the Ten Transferences, and Bodhisattva Vajragarbha expounds the Ten Grounds—each assembly concludes with the adornment of the site of enlightenment, each subsequent one being more excellent than the last, adorned with incalculable numbers (*asaṃkhyeya*) of jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies of various kinds.
It was so that the assembly at that time might universally see bodhisattvas of the same name in the ten directions all speaking of the same practice.

Now, since the World-Honored One himself speaks this sutra, we see that in the ocean-like assemblies of the buddhas throughout the ten directions, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, they all speak in the same way.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:

"What is manifested by the manifesting-consciousness (ādarśa-vijñāna) is also like this.

Furthermore, the subsequent part of the sutra states: "To suddenly discern and know the manifestation of one's own mind as body, as well as the bodies established therein and the objects of enjoyment"—this corresponds respectively to the five sense-objects, such as the physical body, the external environment, and forms, because they manifest spontaneously at all times.
These are the three subtle states, for they are the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
If that is so, what does the term "consciousness" at the beginning of the sutra refer to?
And upon what kind of perfuming (*vāsanā*) does it depend as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for arising?
Answer:
The initial karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) constitutes the first consciousness, as it is established as the sequence according to the gate of origination.

Furthermore, since time from distant kalpas has no beginning, and the past and future lack substantiality, the perfuming (*vāsanā*) is solely mind; deluded thought (*vikalpa*) is the beginning, for it arises in opposition to the Truth (*tattva*).
Furthermore, regarding "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness.
The commentary from Haidong explains:
"The fundamental ignorance perfumes that original enlightenment; this is termed 'inconceivable perfuming'."
The movement that follows from original enlightenment (prakṛtistha-awakening) is called "perfuming" (vāsanā).
Furthermore, although the essence of that original enlightenment is unchanging, it is said to be "changing" because it accords with conditions.
Whether as perfuming or as changing, its path is cut off from mind and speech; thus it is named "inconceivable" (acintya).

Regarding the cause of the manifest consciousness (*nirmāṇa-vijñāna*), this is explained according to its coarse and apparent aspects; however, in terms of its actual principle, it is the causal consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) that serves as the cause.

Furthermore, concerning "causes and conditions," Master Haedong’s commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* explains that although the flow [of consciousness] is uniform, when discussing causes and conditions, the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) acts as the cause and ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the condition for the arising of the karma-consciousness. This differs from [the view of] wood or stone in that it possesses existence, and is consistent with the previous explanation.
From this, the second section clarifies the basis of defilement and purity.
The Sūtra states:
"The defiled and pure [states] acquired at birth each serve as the basis for immeasurable and innumerable defiled and pure consciousnesses."
The commentary states:
"Those acquired at birth that are defiled or pure" arise simultaneously with the body because they are obtained as soon as one is born; these, too, have been acquired since beginningless time.
There are two kinds of defilement: obscured and unwholesome.
Purity is of two kinds: neutral (*avyākṛta*) and wholesome (*kuśala*), because they are acquired simultaneously with birth.

As for the term "respective," it means that from defilement arises defilement and from purity arises purity; this is what is meant by being "respective," just as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) draws forth its concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Regarding the phrase "capable of [benefiting] the immeasurable and innumerable": first, there is the immeasurable number of long kalpas; second, there are the immeasurable numbers of the two types—defiled and pure—that arise.

Regarding the "root of defiled and pure consciousness": because it is acquired in a prior birth, it induces its own subsequent class; as the prior serves as the root for the subsequent, it is termed the "root of consciousness.
As for the "differentiation of the various consciousnesses," this has two meanings.
Some say: The eighth [consciousness] is exclusively pure-neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*), because it is the basis for the destinies and births.
The seventh is also constant, because it is obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*).
The first six [consciousnesses] are intermittent and all pertain to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Only the sixth consciousness increases in both its defiled and pure aspects, because it is the most preeminent among those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) regarding functional phenomena.

Although they arise through mutual perfuming as causes, these [defiled and pure states] arise from seeds that are originally and inherently present; each arises from its own seed as a defiled or pure consciousness, serving as the basis for what follows.
Some say: "Karmic consciousness" refers to the power of ignorance, because the mind moves without awareness.

Based on this moving mind, the evolving consciousnesses arise, which are able to perceive objects; thus, based on these perceiving faculties, the manifesting consciousness arises, which is what is called the ability to manifest all objective realms.

Based upon the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*), the cognitive consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) arises; it discriminates between the defiled and the pure, giving rise to the notions of self and phenomena. Therefore, based upon the cognitive consciousness, the continuous consciousness (*prabandha-vijñāna*) arises; it sustains the past karma of good and evil so that it is not lost, and brings to maturity the retributions of suffering and pleasure in the present and future without error.
Although the first three subtle [afflictions] arise from ignorance, they are categorized as pure and indeterminate because they are non-associated [with the mind].
Although the latter two differ in terms of defilement and purity, or inferiority and superiority, they arise from the former, for karma is their fundamental cause.
Regarding the distinction: karma arises from original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), and original enlightenment serves as the basis of karma.

Karma gives rise to other defiled and pure phenomena, and karma serves as the basis for both the defiled and the pure; therefore, the characteristic of karma is taken as the basis for the defiled and the pure.
If that is so, how many kinds of consciousness are there?
And how does perfuming act as the causal condition for their arising?
Answer:
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Mahāmati!
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of consciousness; explained in detail, there are eight aspects.
The three are: the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vikaalpa-vastu-vijñāna*)."
The commentary by Haidong explains:
"True" refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*); "manifest" refers to the eighth consciousness; and the remaining seven are all termed the "discriminating consciousness of phenomena.
Although the seventh consciousness does not take external objects as its condition, it is called "discriminating phenomena" because it takes the eighth consciousness as its object.
If one is in the presence of a former teacher, there is no need for question and answer.

Furthermore, regarding "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), according to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it is because the manifest consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*nirvikalpa-vastu-vijñāna*) serve as reciprocal causes for one another.

The eighth consciousness acts as the cause for the arising of the seven [consciousnesses], while the former seven, acting as perfumers, in turn regenerate the eighth; this is because they have functioned as reciprocal causes since beginningless time.

Furthermore, regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): its own seeds serve as the cause, and the various objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness serve as the condition, because they are able to combine to produce all defiled and pure consciousnesses.

If one were to claim that the *prajñā* lacks the eight consciousnesses, there would be no scriptural passage to refute such a view; therefore, by citing the textual evidence to explain the terms "defiled" and "pure," one can fully realize the underlying principle.
Otherwise, for what would the "initial consciousness" serve as a designation?
However, the *Ekottarika Āgama* has already spoken of the ālayavijñāna; I have cited this to explain the sūtra, so please examine it closely.
This concludes the second section, which clarifies the extent of matter and mind.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the presentation of the beginning and the end; second, the detailed explanation of matter and mind.
First, regarding the initial part, the presentation of the beginning and the end:
Sūtra:
"From the first moment of an unspeakable kalpa, until the final moment of the vajra.
Commentary:
The previous section cited the process of arising from the subtle to the coarse; this section, however, mentions the beginning and end to clarify that [the intermediate stages] are numerous.
"From the first moment" refers to the aforementioned beginning.
Regarding "unspeakable kalpas," because the duration of birth and death is so vast that it cannot be expressed by the calculation of grains of sand, the sutra simply states "unspeakable."
The phrase "up to the vajra" indicates that this refers to the final meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of a bodhisattva, thereby clarifying its conclusion.

Although practitioners of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) also give rise to this concentration upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it is not explicitly mentioned here because they have not yet reached ultimate perfection.

Regarding "concluding in a single kṣaṇa," this refers to the final moment for a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment when relying on the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the Vajra-like Samādhi.
As for how many arisings and cessations occur within this interval, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "O Mahāmati!..."
"All consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which cannot be known through discursive thought. These are:
the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the continuous flow (*pravāha*), and the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary from Haidong explains:
"As for what is called 'continuous flow,' it refers exclusively to the eighth consciousness.
Because its three characteristics are subtle and hidden, and because its seeds and manifestations continue without interruption, it is termed 'continuous flow.
Since the initial karma-consciousness arises conditioned by ignorance, it is said to be 'birth.'"
Because it continues through long kalpas, it is called "abiding.
Upon reaching the Vajra-samādhi, when one attains equal enlightenment and severs fundamental ignorance in a single thought-moment, this is called the cessation of the flowing stream.

As for the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing: the objects and minds of the remaining seven consciousnesses are coarse and manifest, and are therefore termed "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).
Although the seven [consciousnesses] have eight [objects], they are considered subtle in relation to the sixth; yet because they possess the four afflictions, they are also said to be coarse.

Depending on their own seeds and various objects within that manifest consciousness, the seven arise through the harmony of conditions; this is called "arising through mutual production" (*xiāngshēng*).
"The long-term perfuming over many kalpas is called the abiding of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasthiti*).

Moving from the derivative toward the fundamental, gradually subduing and severing [the afflictions] until the completion of the seventh stage is called the cessation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇanirodha*).

Based on the former [aspect of] arising and ceasing, the basis for delusion and awakening (*bhrānti-avabodhāśraya*) is established; based on the latter [aspect of] arising and ceasing, the basis for defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadānāśraya*) is established. The latter is short while the former is long; this is the distinction between the two.
However, this present text concerns the aforementioned characteristics of arising and ceasing, wherein arising, abiding, and ceasing are all contained therein.
From here begins the second section, which clarifies the expansion of matter and mind;
it is divided into three parts:
Furthermore, regarding the first instance of mind arising from mind,
the Sūtra states:
"There are unspeakably unspeakable numbers of consciousnesses."
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "the consciousness that cannot be spoken of," there are two meanings.
One explanation says:

From the initial moment of conception until the final moment of death, the fundamental consciousness does not abide for even a single instant in the interval between; thus, the arising and ceasing of this consciousness cannot be described [in terms of duration].

To cite its extremes: even from beginning to end within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the Intermediate State of Uninterrupted Suffering (*avīci*), there are unspeakable [karmas], let alone throughout long eons—how could one possibly describe all such karma?
Some say:

From the initial arising of the karmic consciousness until its final cessation, throughout the interval—beginningless and endless—there is the creation of karma and the experiencing of its fruits; within the realms, destinies, and births, as one mind arises from another, the momentary succession of all defiled and pure consciousnesses cannot be described. Therefore, the Sūtra states again that it is "inexpressible."
From this second point, matter arises from mind.
The Sūtra says:
"It gives rise to the two dharmas of form and mind in all sentient beings."
The commentary states:

Regarding the production of the two dharmas—form and mind—for all sentient beings, this is explained only in the *Awakening of Faith*. Following the "evolving aspect" (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), the "manifesting aspect" (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*) arises; once the manifest environment appears, there are then the objects of form, which means that form arises after the evolving consciousnesses.
This is also not the case.
The manifest consciousness manifests objects due to the熏 (perfuming) of the preceding six [consciousnesses]; how could it be that the manifest objects arise from the mind?
Does the image within a mirror arise from the mirror itself?

According to the *Vijñaptimātratā*, among the three types of objects, take for instance the "objective realm" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). When color is perfumed within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), the seeds act as the cause; the mind perfumes them, and they manifest from consciousness. What fault is there in color arising from the mind?
This is also not the case. This is because the objects of cognition and their material resistance are each distinct.
Since that which perfumes and that which maintains the seeds both arise from their own respective categories, how could the essence of that which perfumes and maintains be identical to matter?

This is also not the case. Since perfuming and retention depend upon the mind, if the mind does not arise, how can it be called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*)? Furthermore, the third fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"The great element of the conceptualization of moisture gives rise to the internal and external water elements; the great element of the conceptualization of tranquility gives rise to the internal and external fire elements; the great element of the conceptualization of movement gives rise to the internal and external wind elements; and the great element of the conceptualization of the fragmentation of form gives rise to the internal and external earth elements."
Since that sutra states that "the seeds of false conceptualization give rise [to phenomena]," what fault is there in saying that the mind gives rise to form?
If the obstructive and the deliberative were different and necessarily possessed distinct substantial entities, how could one attain the untainted state through cultivation and severance?

Furthermore, when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can contain the great ocean within a single pore or fit Mount Sumeru into a mustard seed, if their physical forms were truly obstructive, how could they not be hindered by those objects?
It is only in relation to deluded perceptions that we speak of obstruction and difference; for those who have attained mastery, there is in reality no difference at all.
This characteristic of mind arises from the mind; the holy teaching states that principle (*nyāya*) serves as the definitive authority.
This concludes the third section: the meaning of the aggregates of form and mind. Sūtra:
"Form is called the aggregate of form; mind is called the four aggregates. Both possess the nature of accumulation and conceal reality.
The commentary states:
Among the five aggregates, the first is the aggregate of form, and the latter four are the aggregates of mind.
"That which is of the nature of accumulation" clarifies the meaning of the *skandhas* (aggregates).
"That which conceals the reality" clarifies the obscuration of the truth.
The essence of the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is profoundly serene; however, because it is concealed by the *skandhas*, it does not manifest.
From here, the second section specifically clarifies the dharma of form (*rūpa*).
This is divided into four parts;
first, we shall clarify the production of form from form.
Sūtra: “Great King!
This single dharma of form gives rise to immeasurable forms.”
The commentary states:
This is a general explanation.
That which is called "form" (rūpa) has the nature of being resistant and obstructive.
From the single aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), since beginningless time, one has received all manner of bodies across the various realms and destinies;
because these arise from their own kind in an infinite succession, this second section clarifies derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Sūtra: "The eye perceives forms; the ear perceives sounds; the nose perceives odors; the tongue perceives tastes; the body perceives tangibles.
Explanation:
To "arise" refers to the faculties grasping their objects; this does not clarify the nature of the faculties themselves.

Regarding the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), their respective categories and enumerations are numerous; their explanations in the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are as commonly interpreted.
From here, the third section clarifies the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that act as creators.
Sūtra:

“That which is firm and stable is called earth; that which is moistening is called water; that which has the nature of warmth is called fire; that which is light and mobile is called wind. Explanation:

Regarding the statement that among the objects of touch there are the four great elements of solidity, cohesion, heat, and motion: "solidity, cohesion, heat, and motion" distinguishes their essential natures, while "earth, water, fire, and wind" enumerates their four names.
"Holding, gathering, ripening, and increasing" distinguish the functions of karma.
Regarding the textual accounts of what has been heard, one should understand that their meanings fall into corresponding categories.
In relation to what was previously created, they serve as conditions; the extent of these conditions should be analyzed as is customary.
From here, the fourth section clarifies the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
The Sūtra states:
"That which serves as the basis for the arising of the five consciousnesses is called the five material sense-faculties."
The commentary states:

Indeed, the five material sense-faculties have pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as their essence. Their physical dimensions, the manner in which they apprehend objects—whether in contact or at a distance—their presence or absence across the various realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*), and their prior abandonment through cultivation, are to be distinguished as usual.
This is the third summary of the antidotes.
The Sūtra says:
"In this manner, proceeding successively, from one form and one mind there arise unspeakably many forms and minds; all are like illusions."
The commentary states:

"Thus evolving in succession" means that from time immemorial, based on a single mental state associated with form (*rūpa-citta*), there arise unspeakably and infinitely many mental states associated with form.
This clarification of their multiplicity is intended to engender a sense of weary detachment (*udvega*); for if they are not remedied and dispelled, one will revolve in saṃsāra for eternal kalpas.
"Because all are like illusions" means causing one to contemplate that form and mind are illusory and unreal, thereby becoming free from all faults and afflictions; this is the antidote.
From here begins the second [section], clarifying the contemplation of the conventional nature of sensation (*vedanā*).
This section is divided into three parts:
first, a general presentation of the designation of feeling; second, an elucidation of the characteristics of the experience of feeling; and third, a demonstration of the remedies.
First, the initial part provides a general presentation of the designation of feeling.
Sūtra:
"Good son! The feelings of sentient beings are established based on worldly convention."
The commentary states:
"Sentient beings" (sattva) refers to those who distinguish them from the five aggregates that are non-sentient.
"Feeling" (vedanā) is the general name for the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha).
If explained separately, it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*) because there is a distinct experiencing; its essence is a mental factor (*caitta*).
Among the universal factors (*mahābhūmika*), feeling is a designation based on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The "appropriated" (upātta) and the "appropriative aggregates" (upādāna-skandha): the former is general while the latter is specific; these two are distinct.
Regarding the phrase "established according to convention" (saṃvṛti-prajñapti), the two characters "convention" (saṃvṛti) shall be explained in sequence to clarify that [the object] is not real.
From here, the second section clarifies the characteristics of experiencing [the fruit].
This is divided into two parts;
first, it clarifies the activity of experiencing.
Sūtra:

"Whether existent or non-existent, the arising of sentient beings' deluded thoughts and recollections, as well as their performance of karma and reception of its fruits—all these are termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Explanation:
"Whether existent or non-existent" refers to what is apprehended by sensation (*vedanā*).
Because it apprehends phenomena consisting of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) that are present before one, it is said to be "existent.
Because it takes as its object a real self (*ātman*) or dharmas that are past or future—phenomena that are not present before one and lack substantial reality—it is said to be "non-existent."
Although objects are myriad and diverse, they are all subsumed herein.
That which merely gives rise to the deluded thoughts and recollections of sentient beings clarifies that they undergo the inversion of delusion.

This is because they experience objects—whether existent or non-existent, favorable or adverse—and thereby give rise to various deluded thoughts and various recollections, such as the three natures, according to what is appropriate.
Although the natures of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental application (*manasikāra*) are not themselves feeling (*vedanā*), they are experienced through feeling because they are associated with it.
As for "performing and experiencing the fruit": this refers to karma that is meritorious, non-meritorious, or immovable; therefore, it is called "performing action."
Because it can induce retribution that is concordant with the present life, concordant with subsequent lives, or indefinite, it is called "experiencing the fruit" (*vedanīya-phala*).
Although the essence of karma and its fruit is inconceivable, it is termed "experience" (*vedanā*) because it is that which is experienced.
"All are termed conventional truth" clarifies that they are not real.
From this, the second [section] clarifies the basis upon which sensation depends.
Sūtra:
"All sentient beings of the three realms and six destinies—brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
Explanation:
The term "three realms" refers to the locus upon which experience depends.
The "six destinies" refers to the destinies where one undergoes birth.
"All sentient beings" refers to those who are capable of initiating that experience.
"Brahmins and so forth" clarifies that the experience is a false discrimination.
"Brahmin" (brāhmaṇa) is translated here as "One of Quiescent Will.
"Kṣatriya" refers to the royal caste.
As for "Viśa," this follows the ancient translation; in the new [terminology] it is called "Vaiśya," which means "merchant."
Regarding the term *śūdra*, this follows the ancient translation; the new [translation] is *śūdrā*, which means "farmer.
To "receive" from the four castes refers to understanding their respective superior and inferior qualities and being assigned distinct occupations; all such instances are termed "receiving."
From this third point, the antidote to delusion is revealed.
The Sūtra says:
"The self, persons, cognition, and views, as well as material phenomena and mental phenomena, are like what is seen in a dream."
The commentary states:
"The self, persons, and cognitive views" refer to the experience of inverted delusion.
"Form-dharmas and mind-dharmas" refer to the basis upon which that experience depends.
Feeling arises dependent upon form and mind, giving rise to the inversions of self and dharmas because it apprehends and understands various kinds of false phenomena.
The phrase "like what is seen in a dream" clarifies its lack of reality.

Within a dream one considers things real, yet upon waking they are entirely non-existent; thus the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Until one attains true awakening, one constantly dwells within a dream."
The Buddhas have declared this to be the long night of birth and death.

Therefore, one should know that the performance of actions and the experiencing of their fruits, as well as the coming and going through the realms and destinies, are all like dreams and entirely unreal.
If one attains true awakening, one will understand this for oneself.
From here, the third section clarifies the provisional nature of names;
it is divided into four parts:
Furthermore, first of all, the title is not literal.
The Sūtra says: “Good son!...”
"All names are merely provisional designations.
The commentary explains:
"All" refers to both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as well as mundane and supramundane phenomena; therefore, it is called "all."
Regarding the term "all names," "name" refers to that which expresses and defines.
Because all phenomena vary in ten thousand ways according to different regions, they are called "all names.
The phrase "all are provisionally established" clarifies that they are not real.

Names express the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena; because the mind takes these as its extended object and does not apprehend the actual substance of the phenomenon, they are called "provisional" (*prajñapti*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Names express intrinsic nature."
Why then do you say that the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) cannot be attained?
You speak of fire burning and food failing to satisfy.

If one were to refer to the essence of phenomena, one should have the poor describe many treasuries; therefore, these are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*), established to clarify that there is no reality.
From this second section, the absence of names in the fundamental state is clarified.
The Sūtra states:

“Before the Buddha appeared, within the conventional truth of illusory phenomena, there were no names and no meanings, nor was there any essence or characteristic; there were no names for the three realms, no retributions for good and evil, and no names for the six destinies.”
The commentary states:

Regarding "illusory phenomena of conventional truth," since both the subject (the dharma that receives) and the object (the designation) are like illusions, this clarifies their lack of substantial reality.

As for "without name and without meaning," "name" refers to the signifier and "meaning" refers to the signified; these are established arbitrarily according to worldly sentiment and do not correspond to the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*). Since they are all unreal, it is said that they "do not exist."
Furthermore, worldly conventional discourse censures its faults because it lacks both name and referent.

As for its lack of essential nature and characteristics: conditioned illusory phenomena rely upon various causes and conditions and thus possess no intrinsic nature or characteristics; as with the preceding case of name and referent, it is said that these too do not exist.
Regarding "the absence of the three realms," etc.: it is because, were it not for the Buddha’s teaching, one would not know the upper and lower positions or the dimensions of the three realms.
Regarding "the retribution of good and evil": this refers to what kind of fruit one shall obtain when performing good or evil deeds—the superior or inferior retribution.
Regarding the names of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*): within these six destinies, there are no names for the various distinctions of rebirth, as none of them are known.
From this, thirdly, the establishment by the Buddha is explained.
Sūtra:
"The appearance of all Buddhas is for the sake of sentient beings; they teach the immeasurable names of the three realms, the six destinies, and defilement and purity.
Explanation:
The appearance of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain liberation; thus, they establish various names.
When it is said that they dwell within the three realms, this is to demonstrate the distinctions between the superior and the inferior.
The teaching of the six destinies is for the purpose of showing that which is born.
The teaching of defilement and purity is for the purpose of showing defilement so that it may be severed, and showing purity so that it may be cultivated.
This is because there are immeasurable names for both the mundane and the supramundane.
From this, the fourth section clarifies the characteristics of the antidote.
The Sūtra says:
"In this way, all things are like the sound of an echo."
The commentary states:
"All such things" refers to all worldly and supramundane speech.
"Like the echo of a call" correctly demonstrates the remedy, for all worldly discourses are unreal.
Because the supramundane teachings are cultivated through the relinquishing of signs, they are all like echoes.
From this, the fourth section clarifies the conventional nature of continuity (*saṃtati-prajñapti*).
This is divided into three parts:
Furthermore, first is the characteristic of continuity as a provisional construct.
The Sūtra states:
"All phenomena continue in succession, not abiding for even a single moment."
The commentary states:
Regarding "the continuity of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-saṃtati*): the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are not a single entity, and thus they are called "all phenomena.
Because they arise and perish while undergoing flux, they are said to be "continuous."
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Birth is the characteristic of the continuity of deceptive phenomena; death is the characteristic of the disintegration of deceptive phenomena.
Here, "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to continuity.
"Moments of thought do not abide" correctly clarifies the meaning of the provisional.
From this point, the second section clarifies the meaning of continuity.
The Sūtra says:
"From moment to moment, they are neither identical nor different; arising swiftly and ceasing swiftly, they are neither annihilated nor eternal.
The commentary states:
"From moment to moment, they are neither identical nor different" indicates that the dharmas of arising and ceasing are not fixed as being either identical or different.

"Arising swiftly and ceasing swiftly, neither annihilated nor eternal" explains that the phenomena of arising and ceasing are neither definitively annihilated nor eternal, nor are they identical or distinct.
If one were to hold that the aggregates and so forth do not exist in the past or future, [the sūtra states] they are "not annihilated" because they arise swiftly.
If one were to hold that the essence of the aggregates and so forth is permanent, it would not be permanent because they perish rapidly.
Because they are impermanent, they are not definitively one;
because they are not annihilated, they are not definitively different.
That which is wondrously free from the perversions of annihilationism, eternalism, identity, and difference is called the observation of the conventional continuity (*saṃtati-prajñapti*).
From this, the third [section] concludes by demonstrating the remedy.
Sūtra:
"Because all conditioned phenomena are like a mirage.
The commentary states:
"Like a mirage" refers to an illustration by way of a concrete example.
In spring, as the sun brings forth life and the vapors of the wilds stir, if one were to say they truly exist, they become increasingly absent as one draws nearer;
yet if one were to say they do not exist now, they can still deceive those who are thirsty.
Therefore, the essence of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) is neither existent nor non-existent; it is shown to be unreal, like a mirage.
From this point, the fifth section clarifies dependent designation (apekṣā-prajñapti).
This is divided into two parts:
First, the explanation of conventional designation through dependence; second, the explanation of conventional designation through dependence.
First, regarding the initial explanation of conventional designation through dependence, the Sūtra says:

"All phenomena are mutually dependent; that is to say, the realm of form, the realm of the eye, and the realm of eye-consciousness, up to the realm of phenomena, the realm of the mind, and the realm of mind-consciousness, are like flashes of lightning."
The commentary states:
"All phenomena are mutually dependent" is the general heading.

"Dependent" means relying upon conditions; that is to say, the conditioned phenomena of the aggregates, bases, and elements do not arise in the absence of their requisite conditions, which constitutes mutual dependence.
What are called the form element (*rūpa-dhātu*), the eye element (*cakṣur-dhātu*), and the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñāna-dhātu*) clarify their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
If these three—the faculty, the object, and the consciousness—do not belong to the same temporal plane or if any one of them is missing, consciousness will certainly not arise.

When the object is present before one, the sense faculty is activated, and consciousness correctly cognizes the object; these must mutually rely upon and depend on one another to achieve illumination and understanding.
The subsequent examples cited below all likewise possess the threefold harmony, clearly demonstrating this mutual dependence.
"Like a flash of lightning" means that the fetters do not endure; because they are provisional and unreal, they cease and vanish immediately.
This second point clarifies the provisional nature of form through relative dependence.
Sūtra:
"They are not fixedly dependent on one another; their existence, non-existence, identity, or difference is like a second moon.
Explanation:
"Indeterminacy through mutual dependence" is the initial thesis.

This is because all phenomena depend upon one another for their definitions—such as beauty and ugliness, high and low, long and short—and so forth; since these qualities of form and mind are mutually dependent, they are all indeterminate.
Regarding existence and non-existence, identity and difference: existence does not exist by itself, for it exists only in dependence upon non-existence;
non-existence does not exist by itself, for it exists only in dependence upon existence.
The same applies to identity and difference.
They are mutually defined in relation to one another and possess no fixed essence.
Furthermore, by using the provisional existence to define non-existence, one attains non-existence while existence is dispensed with;
by depending on non-existence to contemplate existence, one establishes existence while non-existence departs.
As they are alternately exchanged, both lack any intrinsic nature.
The same applies to identity and difference.
Thus, a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says: "The world’s false discrimination sees horns upon rabbits and the like."
Not understanding that the "horns" do not exist, one speaks of the non-existence of a rabbit's horns.
When analyzed down to the ultimate atom, the horns are found to be utterly non-existent.
One must depend upon the existence of a phenomenon in order to give rise to the view of its non-existence.
Question:
Regarding this existence and non-existence, do they refer to the same phenomenon at different times, or do two phenomena exist simultaneously in mutual dependence?
Answer:

Existence and non-existence coexist simultaneously by depending upon a single phenomenon; for example, when a ten-foot length is compared to fifteen feet, that same ten-foot length possesses the characteristic of being short, yet when compared to five feet, it lacks the characteristic of being short and instead possesses the characteristic of being long. Therefore, the two characteristics of shortness and length within that single ten-foot length are both non-existent in their own essence.
The sequence of one phenomenon should be understood by analogy with this.
As for the "second moon," it has no substantial reality;
it is seen as a second moon due to an eye disease.
When one eye is open and the other closed, touching with one hand while seeing with the other, one perceives two;
yet when one eye is closed, the other is touched, and the eyes are free from disease, there is no duality.

It is due to the illness of the mind that one falsely perceives existence and non-existence, unity and difference, beauty and ugliness, length and shortness, and so forth. To demonstrate this for the sake of observation, it is like the moon which does not truly exist [as such].
From this, the sixth section clarifies the conventional nature established through conditions.
The Sūtra states:
"All phenomena are conditionally established; the dharmas of the aggregates, bases, and elements are like bubbles upon water."
The commentary states:
"All phenomena are dependently originated" indicates that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Just as a grain produces a sprout depending on soil, water, and so forth, why do you not say it "produces" [the sprout] but rather that it is "established through conditions"? This is because there is a distinction between "arising from a cause" and "being established through conditions.
As for the dharmas of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), they reveal all phenomena.
These three categories encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), for even when speaking only of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), they likewise include everything.

Although these bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) also extend to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), here only the conditioned are taken, as they are established in dependence upon conditions.
"Like bubbles on water" clarifies their lack of substantiality.
When bubbles arise upon water, the bubbles have no real essence; they are phenomena formed through conditions—how could such phenomena be real?
From here, the seventh section clarifies the conventional nature established through causes.
The Sūtra states:

"All phenomena are established through causes; the simultaneous causes and effects, as well as the sequential causes and effects of all sentient beings, and their wholesome and unwholesome deeds across the three periods of time, are like clouds in the sky."
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "all phenomena are produced by causes," this indicates that all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) necessarily arise in dependence upon causes.
Here, the term "produced" (*cheng*) refers to the process of generation.
The former serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), while this serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); this is the distinction between the two.
The phrase "all sentient beings" indicates that these possess causes, thereby excluding other non-sentient things which lack such causal conditions.
Although external plants, grasses, and so forth arise from seeds, these are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and not causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

As for simultaneous cause and effect, it is because within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), all seeds—whether the three natures of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or the myriad practices of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—are fully present.

As in the present body, within a single moment, the manifest arises from the seeds, and the manifest is able to perfuse the seeds; thus, these three factors simultaneously possess two types of cause-and-effect. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "It is like the wick producing the flame, and the flame producing the scorched wick."
"The three dharmas proceed in mutual succession and exist simultaneously with one another.
Just as two bundles of reeds stand leaning against each other at the same time, so too must cause and effect be simultaneous.

As for cause and effect occurring at different times: this refers to seeds within consciousness viewed in relation to each other across time; or when the seed is in the present and the fruit is in a future life, they do not arise together, and are thus called 'different times.'"

Regarding "good and evil across the three periods of time": while the seeds of karma and the seeds of consciousness exist only in the present, the performance of actions and the experiencing of their fruits span the three periods.
The phrase "like clouds in the sky" indicates the application of an antidote.
Just as no form of clouds is seen in a clear sky, yet when conditions meet, thunder and rain pour down in abundance;
so too, though there is no shape within consciousness, when conditions meet, the realms and stages of suffering and joy become manifest.

Furthermore, the existence or non-existence of the seeds of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is like clouds; since the aggregates arise from seeds and are like clouds, they are conventional (*prajñapti*).

Thus, by observing the essence and function of the aggregates through these seven modes, one observes that the names for their essence and function are subject to arising and ceasing because they depend upon the present and the causes; this serves as the antidote to the [false view of] real permanence.
The reception of names and words, the natural emptiness of permanence and annihilation, and the absence of cause—these constitute the seven examples.
This is the second section, which concludes by demonstrating right contemplation.
It is divided into three parts:
Furthermore, first, the first section clarifies the bodhisattva practice.
The Sūtra says: "Good son!..."

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in non-discrimination; they possess neither the marks of 'this' nor 'that,' nor the marks of 'self' nor 'other,' yet they constantly engage in transformative benefit without the mark of transformative benefit.
The commentary states:
This clarifies right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
One who dwells in non-conceptualization possesses the union of meditative concentration and wisdom, because of being non-conceptual.
One who is without the marks of "this" and "that" is so because, through non-conceptualization, there is neither "this" nor "that."
Regarding "the absence of the marks of self and other": because there is no distinction between "this" and "that," self and other are equal, as they lack dualistic characteristics.

Regarding "constantly practicing the benefit of others while remaining without the mark of benefiting others": although the Bodhisattva fulfills his own compassionate heart by benefiting sentient beings, he does not dwell upon the mark [of such action] even while constantly benefiting others.
From this, the second section clarifies the conduct of the foolish.
The Sūtra says:
"Therefore, one should know that the defiled consciousness of the foolish is stained by and attached to the false; it is bound by signs."
The commentary states:

Regarding the term "foolish person" (yufu), it was formerly called "deluded ordinary person" (yuchi fanfu) or "childish ordinary person" (xia'er fanfu). In this present text, the phrasing is abbreviated and simply says "foolish person"; "foolish" (yu) means lacking wisdom.
Regarding the "defiled consciousness" (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*): because it consists of false discrimination due to the dust and grime of beginningless time, it is called "defiled consciousness.

As for "being stained by and attached to the unreal": because one is unable to discern the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), it is like dust and grime adhering to a moist garment; thus it is said to be "stained.
Because one does not understand reality, it is called "unreal."
"Those bound by signs" refers to being bound by the signs of false and illusory phenomena.
As the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Chapter 19) states: "Sentient beings are bound by signs, and also by the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*)."
"Only by skillfully practicing both śamatha and vipaśyanā can one attain liberation from both.
Because they do not understand that objects are merely their own mind, they are constrained by appearances; hence, it is called "bondage by appearances."
From this, the third section concludes by demonstrating correct contemplation.
The Sūtra says:
“The Bodhisattva contemplates and perceives that he is like an illusory person, devoid of essence or characteristics, being merely like a flower in the sky.”
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva clearly perceives," etc., this clarifies that all Bodhisattvas abide in non-discrimination; they clearly perceive conditioned phenomena as being like illusory persons because they lack intrinsic nature or characteristics.
The phrase "merely like flowers in the sky" clarifies that they have no substantial reality.
When one with cataracts sees flowers, those without cataracts see no flowers; though in the same place and at the same time, there is the difference between seeing and not seeing.
The illumination of the aggregates, bases, and elements regarding existence and non-existence is likewise so.
From this, the third section concludes the correct observation.
Sūtra:
"This is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in the benefit of both self and others, observing according to reality.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that when Bodhisattvas are able to observe as described above, they are cultivating the two benefits and performing correct observation.
This is the third benefit gained from hearing the Dharma.
The Sūtra states:

"While this Dharma was being taught, among the immeasurable assembly of humans and devas, there were those who attained the Patience of Subduing (*kṣānti*), the Patience of Emptiness and Non-arising, and [the stages] from the first bhūmi through the second up to the tenth; immeasurable bodhisattvas attained the stage of being 'born only once more' (*ekajātipratibaddha*)."
The commentary states:
By virtue of hearing the Dharma, each attains superior progress.
As for those beyond the kalpa, they advance to attain the Patience of Subjugation (*kṣānti*), which is the stage of the Three Worthies (*traya-śaikṣa*).

Regarding "the patience of emptiness and non-arising": "emptiness" refers to the three kinds of emptiness, along with the patience of non-arising; these two patiences, both in their general and specific aspects, are as previously explained.
As for the mention of "one ground," this refers to the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), because one proceeds through successive advancements up to the tenth ground.

Regarding those who are "in their last birth before Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they possess the body of a Tuṣita Heaven deity because they are honored as being in their final stage of succession.

Chapter Four: The Two Truths (*Dvayasatya-varga*). In explaining this chapter, to clarify its purpose: while the preceding two chapters separately elucidated the fruit and the cause, this one reveals their basis by providing a general exposition of the two truths.
However, in the preceding "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata," the ultimate and conventional truths were briefly clarified within the context of the true nature (dharmatā).
Here, both are fully elucidated; the relationship between the object, the wisdom, and the words follows the same sequence as previously described.

Regarding the title of this chapter, "Explanation of the Two Truths": first is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and second is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). These are the objects of the two types of wisdom and serve as the fundamental basis for all practices.
Because emptiness and existence are elucidated in contrast to one another, they are called the "Two Truths"; this is an explanation based on their numerical designation.

That which is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); their substance arises from conditions and is provisional rather than real, hence it is named conventional truth.
That which is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the true mark of suchness (*tathatā*); its original nature is pure, being real rather than provisional, hence it is named ultimate truth.
The Sūtra speaks of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the first, the conventional, the Sanskrit term is *saṃvṛti*, which carries the meaning of "concealing and revealing.
Dharmapāla explains it as follows:
"The world refers to 'concealment' (*saṃvṛti*) in the sense that it can be destroyed;
the conventional refers to 'manifestation' (*vyavahāra*) in the sense of following worldly currents.
It is like tying a handkerchief and illusorily transforming it into a rabbit and so forth: the appearance of characteristics conceals the real and manifests the conventional."
Based on this, one should understand that "the world" (*loka*) refers to the conventional world, as it possesses two interpretations.
Regarding the term "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*), the older translation was "the primary meaning" (*prathamārtha*).
"Ultimate" (*parama*) means "superior" or "excellent," while "meaning" (*artha*) has two senses:
First is the meaning of the term "object" (*ālambana*); second is the meaning of the term "principle" (*yukti*).
Regarding the meaning of "truth" (*tattva*), it is "superior," which is precisely its "meaning.
Because it is the object of the two wisdoms—dependent and perfected—it is the meaning of "superior wisdom"; this is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.

*Satya* (truth) means reality. When phenomena accord with their actual state and principles accord with their actual nature, such that neither phenomenon nor principle is erroneous, both are termed *satya*.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, *satya* has two meanings:

first, the sense of not deviating from the characteristics as they have been described; second, the sense of reaching the ultimate point through contemplation of these [characteristics]; therefore, it is called *satya*.
This is explained according to the two interpretations as appropriate.

Regarding the explanation based on persons, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is known by superior wisdom is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); that which is known by middling wisdom is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That which is known by both types of wisdom encompasses both emptiness and existence."
Regarding the exposition according to the Dharma: dharmas possess degrees of excellence and inferiority, and they constitute the conventional and the ultimate through their mutual dependence.
Based generally upon the five dharmas, four levels are established:

first, the two truths of the nominal and the real. Vases, armies, forests, and the like are nominally conventional; the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), and so forth, are real as the ultimate truth.

Second, the two truths of phenomena and principle: the coarse phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are the conventional truth, while the subtle principles of the Four Noble Truths are the ultimate truth.

Third, the two truths of the shallow and the deep: the established framework of the Four Noble Truths is the shallow conventional truth, while the profound suchness of the two kinds of emptiness is the ultimate truth.

Regarding the four ways of explicating the intent of the two truths: the *tathatā* of the two emptinesses is the conventional truth that retains its verbal expression; the *dharmadhātu* of the single reality is the ultimate truth where verbal expression ceases.
The first [of these four] is exclusively conventional, the last is exclusively real, and the three intermediate dharmas are both real and conventional.
Since both the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Chapter 9) and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Chapter 6) explain this extensively,

one will come to fully understand— through the text itself— the distinctions regarding the existence or non-existence of the object and cognition, as well as the numbers one or two, as they are analyzed here in this sutra.
Regarding the fourth chapter, it is fully explained according to the text.
To explain the scriptural passage, there are three main divisions:
first, the analysis through question and answer; second, clarifying that the Buddha spoke in common with others; and third, the benefits obtained from hearing the Dharma.
Regarding the first set of questions and answers, it is divided into three parts:

first, the questions and answers concerning the object and wisdom; second, the questions and answers concerning cultivation and realization; and third, the questions and answers concerning principle and phenomena.
These may also be termed the non-duality of the two truths, the non-duality of words and letters, and the non-duality of dharma-gates, as is fully evident in the text.
The initial inquiry concerning the object and the wisdom is divided into two parts:
first, King Prasenajit’s question; second, the Tathāgata’s formal response.
Within the question, there are further three sections:
Furthermore, first is the inquiry into the existence or non-existence of the truths.
The Sūtra states:
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Bhagavān, does conventional truth exist within ultimate truth?
The explanation says:
This question concerns the objective realm.

Because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is eternal and serves as the host, while conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) is subject to arising and ceasing like a guest, the question is asked whether conventional reality exists within the ultimate.
From this follows the second objection concerning the duality and unity of knowledge.
The Sūtra says:
"If one says it does not exist, then knowledge should not be dual; if one says it exists, then knowledge should not be unitary."
The commentary states:
If one says they are "without equal," this constitutes a double refutation.
If the conventional were non-existent, then wisdom would not be twofold; why, then, is it said that there are two types of wisdom, the ultimate and the conventional?
If one were to say that [the objects] exist as distinct entities, then wisdom would not be unitary; why then is there no duality at the time when true wisdom realizes and understands?
To distinguish this according to persons: ordinary beings are deluded regarding the truth, and their wisdom perceives only the conventional;
those of the Two Vehicles perceive the principle and phenomena separately, whether in meditative concentration or in distraction.
For Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), the wisdom of ultimate reality (*tattvajñāna*) is exclusively true;

from the first through the fifth stages, although they realize the ultimate through fundamental realization (*mūla-pramāṇa*) and subsequently attain the conventional through subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), these two wisdoms regarding the ultimate and conventional truths do not coexist simultaneously.
From the eighth stage onward, up to the Buddhas, although there are two objects, the two wisdoms can indeed coexist.
Based on this general principle, in response to the questioner as appropriate:
if one says they do not exist, then conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) should not perceive duality;
if one says they do exist, then ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) should not illuminate unity.
The application of the critique to the object and the response through wisdom differ in this way.
From here follows the third section, the dual conclusion, which asks: "How so?
The Sūtra says:
"What is the meaning of 'one' and 'two,' and what are their respective matters?
The commentary says:

Regarding "one" and "two," there is the case where the object is one and the wisdom is two, and the case where the object is two and the wisdom is one; these are the dual conjunctions of object and wisdom—what are their respective matters?
From this point, the Tathāgata provides the correct response in two parts:
first, the answer regarding the two truths; second, the elucidation of right knowledge.
Regarding the first two truths, the text is divided into two parts:
first, a brief response in prose; second, an extensive explanation in verse.
Within the first part, there are further three sections:
Furthermore, first, regarding the initial clarification of what was previously asked,
the Sūtra records:
The Buddha said:
“Great King!
You have already asked about this meaning during the time of the Dharma of the past Buddha Dragon-Light-King.
The commentary explains:
To cite the reason for the previous inquiry,
this second section provides a brief response to one or two points.
The Sūtra states:
"I now have nothing to say, and you now have nothing to hear; this absence of speaking and hearing is precisely what is called 'one meaning' and 'two meanings.

The commentary states: Regarding "I now have nothing to say," as the *Benji* (Original Record) says: "Where there is speaking and hearing, there is non-identity (*anekatva*); where there is no speaking and no hearing, there is non-duality (*advaya*). This non-identity and non-duality is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
The ancient commentators on this passage offer two interpretations.
One states:
"Non-identity is precisely the Two Truths—the first being the True [Truth] and the second being the Conventional."
Non-duality is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); because it is neither true nor conventional, it is named the ultimate truth.
Second, it is said:

"Not one" refers to the meaning of the distinction between the two truths, while "non-dual" refers to the meaning of the non-distinction between the two truths; there is no third truth apart from these two truths.
Now, another interpretation states:
where there is speaking and listening, it is conventional and thus not one;
where the characteristics of speaking and listening are absent, it is ultimate and thus not two.
Thus, the presence of marks and the absence of marks clarify the identity and difference [of phenomena].
From this follows the third instruction: "Listen attentively as I speak.
The Sūtra says:
"Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
The commentary explains:
"This means to cause [the listener] to listen with careful scrutiny."
From here, the second section explains this extensively through verses.
This is divided into two parts;
first, the Bhagavān speaks the initial verse.
Sūtra:
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses.
Explanation:
This is as explained in the text.
From this point, the second section provides a detailed exposition through verses.
This is divided into two parts:
First, a separate explanation of the two truths; second, a concluding exhortation to correct contemplation.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the two truths, it is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying the essence of the two truths; second, explaining the objects and wisdom in contrast; third, clarifying conventional truth through analogies.
Within the first two truths, the text is further divided into three parts;
first, the initial section clarifies the essence of the two truths.
The Sūtra states:

"The signless ultimate truth is in essence neither produced by itself nor by another; it exists like an illusion through causes and conditions, and is likewise neither produced by itself nor by another.
Explanation: From here on, the first half-line of each of the three verses clarifies the ultimate (paramārtha), while the second half-line clarifies the conventional (saṃvṛti).
Regarding the signless ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): it clarifies the essence of true reality; because it is devoid of those ten signs, it is called "signless.
It is realized by supreme wisdom (*parama-jñāna*), and its essence is truly eternal; therefore, it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*).
The essence is not an agent, whether self or other; this negates the notions of "self" and "what belongs to the self.
Because the essence is not created by oneself, it is said to be "not self";
because it is not created by what belongs to the self, it is said to be "not other."
The self and what belongs to the self are empty because they are not created by them.
That which exists like an illusion through causes and conditions clarifies the essence of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding the phenomena of form and mind, the seeds serve as the cause and the afflictions serve as the secondary condition.
Alternatively, conditioned phenomena arise from conditions because they exist like illusions;
nor do they have an agent, whether self or other, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "By whom were the twelve links of dependent origination created?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not made by a Buddha, nor made by a bodhisattva, nor even made by any person whatsoever. Therefore, phenomena arising through conditions have no agent, whether self or other.
Furthermore, as the treatise states:
"All conditioned phenomena do not arise from themselves, and therefore are not self-created;

they do not arise from another, and therefore are not created by another. As explained previously regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is thus briefly stated that they are also not created by both self and other.

If one were to state it fully, it should also be said that they are neither produced in common nor produced without cause; this is because conditioned phenomena arise from the perfuming of present seeds, are devoid of self and what belongs to a self, and exist like an illusion.
From this, the second section clarifies the existence or non-existence of the essence.
The Sūtra states:

"The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally without nature; it is emptiness like suchness according to the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). All existing things are illusory existents; they are conventionally existent through the collection of the three types of designation."
The commentary states:

"That the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally without nature" means that the true nature of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) is eternally quiescent by itself, having the signless (animitta) as its nature.

That which is the emptiness and suchness of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is precisely this *dharmatā*, which is neither born nor extinguished, and is eternally immutable; therefore, it is called "emptiness-suchness" (*śūnyatā-tathatā*).
As for "all phenomena that exist as illusions," the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) are not one and the same; hence, they are called "all existents" (*sarvabhava*).

Regarding their essence: the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, comprising both matter and mind, are termed "all existents" (*bhava*); because they lack substantial reality, they are called "illusory existents.

As for "conventionally existent through the collection of the three conventions": because they are a collection of the three conventions—dharmas, sensations, and names—they exist yet lack reality, and are thus termed "conventionally existent."
From this, the third section concludes by clarifying emptiness and existence.
The Sūtra says:
"There is no non-existence that is truly non-existent; cessation is the ultimate emptiness. All phenomena exist through causes and conditions; such is the meaning of existence and non-existence."
The commentary states:
"Non-existence of non-existence as ultimate reality" means that both self and dharmas are non-existent; hence it is called "non-existence of non-existence.
The true non-existence of the ultimate mark (lakṣaṇa) is termed "ultimate reality of non-existence."
Regarding "emptiness of the supreme truth of quiescence": because the characteristics of delusion are eternally extinguished, it is called "quiescence.
It is that which is realized by noble wisdom; thus, it is the "supreme emptiness" that transcends all fetters.

Regarding "all phenomena exist through causes and conditions": this clarifies that the aforementioned various modes of existence appear as if they were caused and conditioned, and are therefore termed "existence."
Regarding the meaning of existence and non-existence being thus:
the "non-existence" that concludes ultimate reality refers to non-existence as realized by wisdom;
the "existence" that concludes conventional reality refers to existence as an illusion. Such is the meaning of illusory existence.
From this second pair, the objects and wisdom are clarified.
This is divided into three parts;
first, the primary section clarifies the essence as being both one and two.
Sūtra:
"Existence and non-existence are fundamentally two, like the two horns of an ox; through illuminating understanding one sees they are not two, yet the Two Truths are eternally not identical.
Explanation:
That "there is no inherent duality" clarifies the essence of the truth (*satya*).
Because the conventional exists and the ultimate is non-existent, they are called "existence and non-existence.
Since from the very beginning their natures have mutually supported one another, and their essence is neither identical nor separate, they are said to be "inherently dual."
The analogy of "a cow with two horns" refers to the fact that when conventional wisdom takes the conventional and ultimate truths as its object, it perceives duality.
"Illuminating understanding sees non-duality" clarifies that true wisdom is free from characteristics and transcends all dependence, thereby realizing non-duality.
The two truths are eternally not identical because they are realized and understood as being without dual characteristics.

If the true and the conventional were two distinct things that could be made identical, then the true and conventional truths would be non-dual and there would be nothing to be identified. However, since they are without duality, there is nothing to be identified.
From this, the second section clarifies the elimination of "one" and "two.
The Sūtra says:
"When the mind understands that there is no duality, one cannot find two upon seeking them; it is not that the two truths are one, for even 'one' cannot be found."
The commentary states:
"To understand that the mind perceives non-duality" refers to the realization of clear wisdom.
"Seeking duality and finding it unobtainable" refers to the elimination of duality.
When wisdom directly realizes suchness, one cannot find any distinct characteristics between the two aspects of ultimate and conventional truth.
This does not mean that each of the two truths is individually unfindable; rather, this negates their being a single [identical] entity.
It does not mean that there is a single reality within non-duality upon realizing suchness; even if one seeks its single characteristic, it cannot be found.
From this, the third [point] concludes the unity of the two.
Sūtra:
"In understanding, there is always only one; in the truths, there are always two. To thoroughly comprehend this oneness and duality is to truly enter the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The commentary states:
This clarifies the oneness and duality of object and wisdom within the preceding question.
Regarding "understanding that it is always one": non-conceptual wisdom understands that the characterized and the uncharacterized are always one.
Regarding "the truths are always two": with respect to the ultimate and conventional truths, one does not maintain that understanding them as one means they are not two.
To thoroughly comprehend this unity and duality is to comprehend the truth of wisdom: because it is conventional, it is not one; because it is ultimate, it is not two.
To truly enter the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) means that "true" is the realization through wisdom.
Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*): it is the realization that the truth of wisdom has no fixed duality or unity; this is the true realization.
From here, the third analogy clarifies conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
This section is divided into two parts:
Furthermore, the first of the initial metaphors clarifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The Sūtra says:
"The conventional truth arises as an illusion, like flowers in the sky, like shadows, or like the optical illusion of floating hairs; it exists illusorily due to causes and conditions."
The commentary states:
"That which arises as an illusion in conventional truth" generally clarifies that all conditioned phenomena arise as illusions.
The following two lines specifically cite three metaphors.
The analogy of "flowers in the sky" illustrates that which exists only through delusion; it refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), for it lacks any substantial reality.

The statement "like a shadow" means that shadows in water, mirrors, and so forth are all produced in dependence upon a substance; this illustrates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), for it manifests due to karmic conditions.
The phrase "like a net of hairs" serves to clarify what precedes it.
Because of the presence of an optical impairment (*timira*), one perceives a net of hairs; if the optical impairment were absent, both [the perception and the object] would be non-existent.
Due to the delusion of the mind, one falsely perceives the former two; if wisdom realizes suchness, both are absent.

Regarding the statement that things exist as illusions due to causes and conditions: this concludes that worldly conventional phenomena exist like illusions by virtue of resembling causes and conditions.
From this point, the second section begins by citing the illusion.
The Sūtra states:

"When one illusory being sees another illusory being, the foolish call it a 'real illusion. When an illusionist sees his illusory phenomena, both the reality and the illusion are entirely non-existent."
The commentary states:
"A magical creation seeing a magical creation" clarifies that all things in the world—both the subject that sees and the object that is seen—are entirely unreal, for they are but magical creations.

"Fools call it the 'truth of illusion'" means that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), being ignorant and lacking the eye of wisdom, constantly dwell within illusion; thus, it is called the "truth of illusion."
"The illusionist who perceives illusory phenomena" refers to Bodhisattvas who have attained the illusory body and are thus able to see that the conventional truth is illusory and unreal.
"When both truth and illusion are entirely non-existent" means they have realized the emptiness of persons and phenomena, such that all things are utterly non-existent.
From this point, the second section provides a summary exhortation for correct contemplation.
The Sūtra says:
"If one thoroughly understands such dharmas as these, one will understand the meaning of 'one' and 'two'."
"One should contemplate all phenomena in this manner.
The commentary states:
